title: Digital Auditing & Assurance (CA Final – Audit)
description: CA Final – Auditing and Professional Ethics: application-oriented MCQ bank on Digital Auditing & Assurance, covering digital audit and understanding the IT environment, risks arising from use of IT, IT dependencies and General IT Controls, cyber risks and their stages, the cyber security framework and control considerations, emerging technologies (IoT, AI, Blockchain, NFT, RPA), remote audit, auditing digitally, data analytics and CAATs, technology risks and control considerations, and next generation audit (drone, AR, VR, metaverse). Includes case-study, multiple-statement, assertion–reason, matching, sequence and integrated multi-concept formats; each question is independently usable.

questions.question:
Case Study A. CA Meera is the engagement partner for the statutory audit of Ujjaini Motors Ltd for FY 2025-26, an auto-component manufacturer. The company uses SAP for manufacturing and inventory, a Tally installation for compiling the financial statements, an in-house Excel depreciation workbench, a biometric attendance device linked to a payroll application hosted by a service provider, and drones to count stock in two warehouse sheds. The CFO argues that a 'digital audit' must simply mean faster vouching. During planning, a team member proposes to document only the names of the applications, treating organisation structure, governance and the policies and procedures followed as irrelevant because they are not accounting records. Another proposes to complete the reading of the purchase and sales flows entirely before beginning to think about which systems are significant, since a strict sequence is tidier. The draft internal-control listing records only manual checks, such as the stores in-charge's signed gate pass, and omits the edits and validations built into SAP. The team is also doubtful whether the complexity of the IT environment should be assessed once for the company as a whole or application by application.

Statement 1: The proposal to document only the names of applications leaves out at least two of the items that the source says an auditor's understanding of an automated environment should include.
Statement 2: Where an application is hosted by a service provider, organisation structure and governance need not be understood, because governance of that application rests with the provider.
Statement 3: Details of IT infrastructure components are to be understood for each application, and not merely for the entity as a single undifferentiated environment.
Statement 4: IT risks and controls form part of the required understanding, whereas the policies, procedures and processes followed do not.

Which of the above statements correctly reflect what the auditor's understanding of the automated environment should include?
options: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The source lists five things the auditor's understanding of an automated environment should include: the applications used by the company, details of IT infrastructure components for each application, organisation structure and governance, the policies, procedures and processes followed, and IT risks and controls. Statement 1 is therefore correct: naming applications omits the infrastructure, governance, policy and risk-and-control items. Statement 3 is correct because the source expressly ties infrastructure detail to 'each application', which is why the payroll application hosted by the provider and the in-house Excel workbench cannot be lumped together. Statement 2 is incorrect, since the source states organisation structure and governance as an unconditional component and the hosting arrangement does not remove the payroll application from the list of applications being used by the company. Statement 4 is incorrect because it splits the list arbitrarily: policies, procedures and processes are named alongside IT risks and controls. The decisive fact is that the source's five items are cumulative, so a plan documenting only application names is deficient on four counts.

questions.question:
Case Study A. CA Meera is the engagement partner for the statutory audit of Ujjaini Motors Ltd for FY 2025-26, an auto-component manufacturer. The company uses SAP for manufacturing and inventory, a Tally installation for compiling the financial statements, an in-house Excel depreciation workbench, a biometric attendance device linked to a payroll application hosted by a service provider, and drones to count stock in two warehouse sheds. The CFO argues that a 'digital audit' must simply mean faster vouching. During planning, a team member proposes to document only the names of the applications, treating organisation structure, governance and the policies and procedures followed as irrelevant because they are not accounting records. Another proposes to complete the reading of the purchase and sales flows entirely before beginning to think about which systems are significant, since a strict sequence is tidier. The draft internal-control listing records only manual checks, such as the stores in-charge's signed gate pass, and omits the edits and validations built into SAP. The team is also doubtful whether the complexity of the IT environment should be assessed once for the company as a whole or application by application.

Statement 1: The auditor may identify significant IT applications concurrently with understanding how financial information flows through the entity's information system, so the strictly sequential plan is not required by the source.
Statement 2: Under 'understand flow of transaction', the auditor is concerned with the nature of the IT applications relevant to the flow of transactions, their number being an IT department matter.
Statement 3: Because the payroll application is hosted by a service provider rather than run in-house, it stands outside the flow of transactions and so need not be considered in identifying systems.
Statement 4: The listing that captures only the signed gate pass is complete for the source's purposes, because the SAP edits are automated and hence self-evidently reliable.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: Statements 1 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the source expressly says the auditor 'may identify IT application concurrently with his understanding of how financial information flows through entity's information system', so the team's insistence on completing the flow work first has no basis in the key areas. Statement 2 is not correct, because the source directs the auditor to the 'nature and number of IT applications relevant to flow of transactions in information system'; number is the auditor's concern, not the IT department's. Statement 3 is not correct, since the source's understanding list speaks of applications 'being used by company' and of infrastructure components 'for each application'; where the software is installed is not the test. Statement 4 is not correct, because the source says the entity's system of internal control contains manual and automated elements and that identification of both is relevant to the identification and assessment of ROMM - omitting the SAP edits leaves that identification incomplete. The decisive facts are the words 'nature and number' and 'concurrently', which the team's plan ignores.

questions.question:
Case Study A. CA Meera is the engagement partner for the statutory audit of Ujjaini Motors Ltd for FY 2025-26, an auto-component manufacturer. The company uses SAP for manufacturing and inventory, a Tally installation for compiling the financial statements, an in-house Excel depreciation workbench, a biometric attendance device linked to a payroll application hosted by a service provider, and drones to count stock in two warehouse sheds. The CFO argues that a 'digital audit' must simply mean faster vouching. During planning, a team member proposes to document only the names of the applications, treating organisation structure, governance and the policies and procedures followed as irrelevant because they are not accounting records. Another proposes to complete the reading of the purchase and sales flows entirely before beginning to think about which systems are significant, since a strict sequence is tidier. The draft internal-control listing records only manual checks, such as the stores in-charge's signed gate pass, and omits the edits and validations built into SAP. The team is also doubtful whether the complexity of the IT environment should be assessed once for the company as a whole or application by application.

Concept 1: Identification of Manual and Automated Controls, because the entity's system of internal control contains both manual and automated elements.
Concept 2: Identification of Technologies Used, which requires understanding the emerging technologies implemented and considering whether risks arise from their use.
Concept 3: Assessing Complexity of IT Environment, on the footing that complexity is a single attribute of the environment as a whole.
Concept 4: Understand Flow of Transaction, directed to the nature and number of IT applications relevant to that flow.

Which combination correctly identifies the key areas that the draft plan fails to discharge on the facts above?
options: Concepts 1, 2 and 4 only
Concepts 1 and 3 only
Concepts 2, 3 and 4 only
Concepts 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Concept 1 applies: the listing captures only the gate pass and omits the SAP edits and validations, so the automated element of internal control is unaddressed and, with it, the input to identifying and assessing ROMM. Concept 2 applies: the biometric device and the drones are emerging technologies implemented in the entity, and the source requires the auditor to understand them and consider whether risks arise from their use, which the plan does not do. Concept 4 applies, since the plan documents application names rather than the nature and number of applications relevant to the flow of transactions. Concept 3 does not apply as worded, because the source states that not all applications have the same level of complexity and that the level of complexity for individual characteristics differs across applications - the team's 'once for the company' premise is the error, not the area itself. The decisive point is that an incorrectly stated concept must not be selected merely because the underlying area is relevant.

questions.question:
Case Study A. CA Meera is the engagement partner for the statutory audit of Ujjaini Motors Ltd for FY 2025-26, an auto-component manufacturer. The company uses SAP for manufacturing and inventory, a Tally installation for compiling the financial statements, an in-house Excel depreciation workbench, a biometric attendance device linked to a payroll application hosted by a service provider, and drones to count stock in two warehouse sheds. The CFO argues that a 'digital audit' must simply mean faster vouching. During planning, a team member proposes to document only the names of the applications, treating organisation structure, governance and the policies and procedures followed as irrelevant because they are not accounting records. Another proposes to complete the reading of the purchase and sales flows entirely before beginning to think about which systems are significant, since a strict sequence is tidier. The draft internal-control listing records only manual checks, such as the stores in-charge's signed gate pass, and omits the edits and validations built into SAP. The team is also doubtful whether the complexity of the IT environment should be assessed once for the company as a whole or application by application.

Action 1: Add the SAP edits and validations to the control listing, treating their identification as relevant to identifying and assessing ROMM along with the manual gate-pass check.
Action 2: Record, as part of identifying technologies used, that biometrics and drones are among the source's examples of emerging technologies, and consider whether risks arise from their use.
Action 3: Assess complexity characteristic by characteristic for each application, rather than issuing one company-wide complexity rating.
Action 4: Confine the understanding of the automated environment to applications that post entries directly to the financial statements, because only those are relevant to the flow of transactions.

Which combination of actions is consistent with the source?
options: Actions 1 and 4 only
Actions 2 and 4 only
Actions 1, 2 and 3 only
Actions 1, 2, 3 and 4
questions.explanation: Action 1 follows directly from the source's statement that internal control contains manual and automated elements and that identification of both is relevant to the auditor's identification and assessment of ROMM. Action 2 matches the key area on identification of technologies used, which lists blockchain, robotics, artificial intelligence, internet of things, biometrics and drone as examples and requires the auditor to consider whether risks arise from their use. Action 3 is required because the source says not all applications have the same level of complexity and that the level for individual characteristics differs across applications - the in-house Excel workbench and SAP plainly are not comparable. Action 4 is inconsistent: 'relevant to flow of transactions' narrows one key area, whereas the source's list of what the auditor's understanding should include extends to applications used by the company, infrastructure for each application, organisation structure and governance, policies, procedures and processes, and IT risks and controls. The decisive fact is that the payroll application and the drones are used by the company even though neither posts a journal entry.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Meaning and Key Features
questions.question:
Case Study A. CA Meera is the engagement partner for the statutory audit of Ujjaini Motors Ltd for FY 2025-26, an auto-component manufacturer. The company uses SAP for manufacturing and inventory, a Tally installation for compiling the financial statements, an in-house Excel depreciation workbench, a biometric attendance device linked to a payroll application hosted by a service provider, and drones to count stock in two warehouse sheds. The CFO argues that a 'digital audit' must simply mean faster vouching. During planning, a team member proposes to document only the names of the applications, treating organisation structure, governance and the policies and procedures followed as irrelevant because they are not accounting records. Another proposes to complete the reading of the purchase and sales flows entirely before beginning to think about which systems are significant, since a strict sequence is tidier. The draft internal-control listing records only manual checks, such as the stores in-charge's signed gate pass, and omits the edits and validations built into SAP. The team is also doubtful whether the complexity of the IT environment should be assessed once for the company as a whole or application by application.

Statement 1: The CFO's reading is narrower than the source's meaning, since a digital audit places assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems implemented in the organisation.
Statement 2: A key feature is that it improves the quality of the opinion, which the source links to a more reliable audit report.
Statement 3: Among the listed key features are that it encourages the auditee to embrace the latest technological advancements and that it can help the auditee make informed decisions.
Statement 4: Because the source lists savings in time and cost, it treats a reduction in the overall audit cost as the necessary consequence of a digital audit.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: Statements 1 and 4 only
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
All of the statements
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: The source defines digital audit as placing assurance on the effectiveness of IT systems implemented in the organisation; that object is about the IT systems themselves, not merely about speeding up vouching, so statement 1 is right and the CFO's reading is too narrow. Statements 2 and 3 reproduce key features as listed - improvement in the quality of the opinion leading to a more reliable audit report, encouragement to embrace the latest technological advancements, and help to the auditee in making informed decisions. Statement 4 is incorrect because the source's language is conditional: shortening the time to complete the audit 'may' lower the audit's overall cost, and the time and cost saved are said to be capable of being utilised for more productive tasks. The decisive fact is the modal verb in the advantage, which stops a possibility being represented to the CFO as a certainty.

questions.question:
Case Study B. Kanchan Spinning Mills Ltd decided to automate its accounts-payable invoice matching. The IT head selected the tool on technical grounds without asking management what business benefit the company wanted from the automation. The matching process itself worked differently in each of the four plants and had never been documented or standardised, yet it was automated plant-wise exactly as it stood. The twelve clerks whose data-entry work was displaced learned of the change only after go-live, and two of them now override the bot informally; the HR head has described the change as merely a software purchase. The CFO expects the audit fee to fall, better trend and pattern information for the board, and hopes the auditors will use the resulting data to concentrate testing where assessed risk is highest. In the post-implementation review the company's security team flagged that vendor-supplied access to the automation console had never been reviewed.

Statement 1: Knowing what business benefit the organisation wants to achieve with automation is one of the listed considerations, and the IT head's approach ignores it.
Statement 2: Automating each plant's own variant of the process is permissible once the right tool has been chosen, because standardisation is a precondition of manual working only.
Statement 3: 'Think people first' and do not underestimate that change is difficult are listed considerations, and the way the clerks were handled is inconsistent with them.
Statement 4: The security team's flag relates to the challenge the source identifies with data security and governance.

Which of the above statements correctly apply the source's considerations and challenges to these facts?
options: Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
Statements 1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The source lists five considerations and challenges: knowing the business benefits the organisation wants from automation, thinking people first and not underestimating that change is difficult, choosing the right tool and automating the right process, ensuring the process works and is standardised before automating, and challenges with data security and governance. Statements 1, 3 and 4 each match one of these to a specific fact - the unanswered business-benefit question, the post-go-live treatment of the clerks, and the unreviewed vendor access to the console. Statement 2 is wrong because it inverts the source's order: the requirement is to ensure the process works and is standardised before automating, and choosing the right tool is a separate, additional consideration rather than a substitute for it. The decisive fact is that four undocumented and differing plant processes were automated as they stood, which is the precise situation the source warns against.

questions.question:
Case Study B. Kanchan Spinning Mills Ltd decided to automate its accounts-payable invoice matching. The IT head selected the tool on technical grounds without asking management what business benefit the company wanted from the automation. The matching process itself worked differently in each of the four plants and had never been documented or standardised, yet it was automated plant-wise exactly as it stood. The twelve clerks whose data-entry work was displaced learned of the change only after go-live, and two of them now override the bot informally; the HR head has described the change as merely a software purchase. The CFO expects the audit fee to fall, better trend and pattern information for the board, and hopes the auditors will use the resulting data to concentrate testing where assessed risk is highest. In the post-implementation review the company's security team flagged that vendor-supplied access to the automation console had never been reviewed.

The CFO asks the auditors whether the automation should have proceeded in the order in which it was done. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate response under the source?
options: The order is unobjectionable, since automating first is the recognised way to force divergent plant processes to converge.

The order is objectionable: the source's consideration is that the process must work and be standardised before it is automated, and choosing the right tool and automating the right process is a separate consideration.
The order is objectionable only to the extent the automated process produces information used in financial reporting, since the source's considerations address that population alone.
The order is unobjectionable provided the auditee embraces the latest technological advancements, that being the substance of a digital audit.
questions.explanation: The source states the considerations in a sequence of preconditions: know the business benefit wanted, think people first, choose the right tool and automate the right process, and ensure the process works and is standardised before automating. On these facts the standardisation precondition was skipped for all four plants, which is why two clerks can still override the bot - an automated version of four different processes is not one controlled process. Option 1 states the position accurately and captures both that standardisation precedes automation and that tool selection is a distinct consideration. Option 2 wrongly narrows the considerations to financial-reporting data, a limitation the source does not impose. Option 0 adds a proposition - that automating first will force divergent plant processes to converge - for which the source gives no support, and option 3 substitutes a key feature of digital audit for a precondition about process design.

questions.question:
Case Study B. Kanchan Spinning Mills Ltd decided to automate its accounts-payable invoice matching. The IT head selected the tool on technical grounds without asking management what business benefit the company wanted from the automation. The matching process itself worked differently in each of the four plants and had never been documented or standardised, yet it was automated plant-wise exactly as it stood. The twelve clerks whose data-entry work was displaced learned of the change only after go-live, and two of them now override the bot informally; the HR head has described the change as merely a software purchase. The CFO expects the audit fee to fall, better trend and pattern information for the board, and hopes the auditors will use the resulting data to concentrate testing where assessed risk is highest. In the post-implementation review the company's security team flagged that vendor-supplied access to the automation console had never been reviewed.

Statement 1: The CFO's hope about trend and pattern information corresponds to the source's advantage of better analytics, which aids management and auditors in seeing trends and patterns.
Statement 2: The CFO's hope about concentrating testing where risk is highest is supported by the advantage of improved risk assessment, under which management and auditors put their testing efforts on higher ROMM areas and make informed decisions.
Statement 3: Enhanced effectiveness and efficiency is attributed by the source to the saving of time and cost that comes from automating routine tasks.
Statement 4: Better audit quality under the source consists in the elimination of the chance of misstatement, and lower cost is stated as a certainty where audit time shortens.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: Statement 4 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 each reproduce an advantage as the source frames it: better analytics is described in terms of aiding management and auditors in seeing trends and patterns, improved risk assessment in terms of management and auditors putting their testing efforts on higher ROMM areas and making informed decisions, and enhanced effectiveness and efficiency in terms of automated routine tasks saving time and cost. Statement 4 is the only statement that is not correct, and it is wrong on both of its halves. The source says better audit quality consists in lowering the chance of misstatements, not in eliminating that chance, and it says shortening the time to complete the audit may lower the audit's overall cost, so the cost outcome is stated as a possibility rather than a certainty. The decisive words are therefore lowering and may, and the CFO's expectation of a guaranteed fee reduction and an immune financial statement both overstate them. A candidate must distinguish a reduction in probability from removal, and a possibility from a promise.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question:
Case Study C. Sundari Retail Ltd operates three brands. In the revenue cycle the auditor counted nine IT applications - a point-of-sale application at each brand, two warehouse applications, an e-commerce storefront, a payment gateway, a loyalty-points application and the general ledger - while the payroll cycle runs on one hosted application. The audit team proposes to describe the revenue cycle as 'nine systems, all equally simple' because none of them is an ERP, and to record only that the storefront is 'online'. The engagement memo states that because the flow of transactions is now understood, no separate thought is needed about which systems are significant. Management, having agreed to a digital audit, has asked the auditors to confirm that automating routine work will guarantee lower fees and that no misstatement can now arise, and has asked that extra testing effort be spread evenly across all cycles rather than concentrated where assessed risk is highest.

Statement 1: Under 'understand flow of transaction', both the nature and the number of IT applications relevant to the flow of transactions call for identification and understanding.
Statement 2: The count of nine revenue-cycle applications against one payroll application is itself a relevant observation for the auditor under that area.
Statement 3: Once the flow of transactions is understood, the separate key area of identifying significant systems is thereby discharged.
Statement 4: Rating every application as equally simple is consistent with the source, complexity turning on whether an application is an ERP.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
questions.explanation: The source directs the auditor to identify and understand the nature and number of IT applications relevant to the flow of transactions in the information system, so both the design and the count of the nine applications are within the area, which makes statements 1 and 2 correct. Statement 3 is incorrect: identification of significant systems is listed as a separate key area, and although it may be performed concurrently with understanding how financial information flows, concurrency is not absorption. Statement 4 is incorrect because the source says not all applications have the same level of complexity and that the level of complexity for individual characteristics differs across applications; ERP status is not the test offered. The decisive facts are the words 'nature and number' in one cell and 'individual characteristics differs across applications' in the other, both of which the team's memo overrides.

questions.question:
Case Study C. Sundari Retail Ltd operates three brands. In the revenue cycle the auditor counted nine IT applications - a point-of-sale application at each brand, two warehouse applications, an e-commerce storefront, a payment gateway, a loyalty-points application and the general ledger - while the payroll cycle runs on one hosted application. The audit team proposes to describe the revenue cycle as 'nine systems, all equally simple' because none of them is an ERP, and to record only that the storefront is 'online'. The engagement memo states that because the flow of transactions is now understood, no separate thought is needed about which systems are significant. Management, having agreed to a digital audit, has asked the auditors to confirm that automating routine work will guarantee lower fees and that no misstatement can now arise, and has asked that extra testing effort be spread evenly across all cycles rather than concentrated where assessed risk is highest.

Which of the following representations by the auditor to management is LEAST appropriate?
options: Automating routine tasks saves time and cost, and shortening the time to complete the audit may lower its overall cost.
Digital audit improves the quality of the opinion, which leads to a more reliable audit report.
Better analytics under a digital audit aids management and auditors in seeing trends and patterns.
Where routine processing is automated, the assessed risks of material misstatement for the affected cycles need not be revisited.
questions.explanation: Options 0, 1 and 2 are all supported by the source: lower cost is expressed as a possibility arising from shortened audit time, improved quality of the opinion is linked to a more reliable audit report, and better analytics is described in terms of trends and patterns. Option 3 is least appropriate because the source treats identification of both manual and automated controls as relevant to the auditor's identification and assessment of ROMM, and lists IT risks and controls among the things the auditor must understand about an automated environment; automation changes the character of the risk, it does not remove the need to assess it. The decisive fact is that the same source whose advantages the auditor wishes to claim also makes ROMM assessment dependent on identifying automated elements. Note that options 0 and 2 are properly hedged whereas option 3 converts an advantage into a dispensation from a required assessment.

questions.question:
Case Study C. Sundari Retail Ltd operates three brands. In the revenue cycle the auditor counted nine IT applications - a point-of-sale application at each brand, two warehouse applications, an e-commerce storefront, a payment gateway, a loyalty-points application and the general ledger - while the payroll cycle runs on one hosted application. The audit team proposes to describe the revenue cycle as 'nine systems, all equally simple' because none of them is an ERP, and to record only that the storefront is 'online'. The engagement memo states that because the flow of transactions is now understood, no separate thought is needed about which systems are significant. Management, having agreed to a digital audit, has asked the auditors to confirm that automating routine work will guarantee lower fees and that no misstatement can now arise, and has asked that extra testing effort be spread evenly across all cycles rather than concentrated where assessed risk is highest.

Response 1: The source's advantage of improved risk assessment is precisely that management and auditors put their testing efforts on higher ROMM areas, so even spreading is contrary to it.
Response 2: Identifying the manual and automated elements of internal control is relevant to the identification and assessment of ROMM, which supplies the basis on which cycles are ranked.
Response 3: A key feature of a digital audit is that it can help the auditee to make informed decisions, which is consistent with directing effort by assessed risk rather than evenly.
Response 4: Since the source lists savings in time and cost among the key features, effort should be levelled so that the engagement remains simple enough to deliver those savings.

Which of the above responses appropriately meet management's last request?
options: Responses 1 and 3 only
Responses 2 and 4 only
Responses 1, 2 and 3 only
Responses 1, 2, 3 and 4
questions.explanation: The source states improved risk assessment as an advantage under which management and auditors put their testing efforts on higher ROMM areas and make informed decisions, so response 1 answers management's request directly. Response 2 supplies the mechanism: the identification of both manual and automated elements of internal control is relevant to identifying and assessing ROMM, and without it there is no defensible ranking of the nine revenue applications against the single payroll application. Response 3 reinforces the same conclusion from the key features, which say a digital audit can help the auditee make informed decisions. Response 4 is wrong because it converts a stated feature - savings in time and cost that can be utilised for more productive tasks - into a reason to level effort, whereas the source's own logic is that saved effort is redeployed to higher-risk areas. The decisive fact is that even spreading is the opposite of the source's stated advantage.

questions.question: While planning the digital audit of Trishul Engineering Ltd, the incoming manager proposes the following order of work: first assess the risks arising from the IT environment, then identify the significant applications, and finally understand the applications, infrastructure, governance, policies and IT controls - arguing that assessment can be done first because it drives the whole plan. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of the stages involved in a digital audit as given in the source?
options: Identify - Understand - Assess
Understand - Identify - Assess
Assess - Understand - Identify
Understand - Assess - Identify
questions.explanation: The source states that the stages involved in digital audit are Understand, Identify and Assess, in that order, so the manager's proposal reverses the first and third stages. The sequence is also internally coherent with the key areas: the five things the auditor's understanding should include - applications, infrastructure components for each application, organisation structure and governance, policies, procedures and processes, and IT risks and controls - belong to the understand stage, while identification of significant systems, of manual and automated controls and of technologies used belongs to the identify stage which follows it. Option 0 wrongly supposes the auditor can identify systems before understanding the environment, and option 2 adopts exactly the manager's error. Option 3 places assessment before identification, which leaves the assessment without the control population that the source ties to ROMM identification. The decisive fact is the source's explicit three-stage order, which is not a matter of engagement preference.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Features and Advantages
questions.question:
Column I lists attributes of a digital audit as stated in the source; Column II lists the consequence the source attaches to each.
Column I: A. Improves quality of opinion. B. Better Analytics. C. Enhanced Effectiveness & Efficiency. D. Improved Risk Assessment.
Column II: 1. Automated routine task saves time and cost. 2. Leads to more reliable audit report. 3. Testing efforts are put on higher ROMM areas and informed decisions are made. 4. Aids management and auditors in seeing trends and patterns.

Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: The source places 'improves quality of opinion' among the key features and says this leads to a more reliable audit report, so A-2. Better analytics is stated as an advantage that aids management and auditors in seeing trends and patterns, so B-4. Enhanced effectiveness and efficiency is expressly attributed to automated routine tasks saving time and cost, so C-1. Improved risk assessment is stated as management and auditors putting their testing efforts on higher ROMM areas and making informed decisions, so D-3. The trap is C-4 or B-1: both concern analytics and both concern time and cost, but analytics is about trend and pattern information while efficiency is about the labour saved by automation. A second trap is pairing A with D, because the reliability of the report and the direction of testing effort are consequences of different items and belong respectively to the feature list and the advantage list.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The auditor must complete his understanding of how financial information flows through the entity's information system before he begins to identify the significant IT applications.
Reason (R): The source indicates that the auditor may identify the IT application concurrently with his understanding of how financial information flows through the entity's information system.

Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are correct, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is correct, but R is incorrect.
A is incorrect, but R is correct.
questions.explanation: The reason restates the source's cell on identification of significant systems, which uses the word 'concurrently', so R is correct. The assertion asserts the opposite - a strict sequence in which flow understanding must be finished first - and therefore contradicts the very source on which it purports to rely, so A is incorrect. Because A is wrong, the options that begin by treating both as correct cannot be reached, and the logical-relationship analysis becomes unnecessary. The decisive fact is that the source permits the two activities to be performed in parallel, so an engagement plan that defers identification of significant systems until the flow work is closed imposes a discipline the source does not require. Note that concurrency does not make identification unnecessary, which is a separate error made elsewhere in the same study scheme.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A control listing that captures only the manual checks operated by the entity is, on the source's own terms, sufficient input to the auditor's identification and assessment of ROMM.
Reason (R): The entity's system of internal control contains manual and automated elements, and the identification of both is relevant to the auditor's identification and assessment of ROMM.

Which of the following is correct?
options: A is incorrect, but R is correct.
Both A and R are correct, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are correct, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is correct, but R is incorrect.
questions.explanation: The reason reproduces the source's cell on identification of manual and automated controls and is therefore correct. The assertion draws the opposite conclusion from it: if identification of both elements is relevant to identifying and assessing ROMM, then a listing that captures only manual checks is incomplete by the source's own test, so A is incorrect. Once A is shown to be incorrect, the two options requiring both statements to be true fail, as does the option that treats R as wrong. The decisive fact is the word 'both' in the source, which converts the presence of automated elements such as system edits from an optional detail into a required identification. The point matters most in a heavily automated environment, where the manual residue in a listing can look complete while excluding the controls that actually operate.

questions.question:
Statement 1: The auditor's understanding of an automated environment includes the applications being used by the company and the details of IT infrastructure components for each application.
Statement 2: Organisation structure and governance are left out of the understanding, being entity-level rather than IT matters.
Statement 3: The policies, procedures and processes followed by the entity form part of the understanding of the automated environment.
Statement 4: IT risks and controls are to be understood only where the auditor intends to rely on automated controls.

Which of the above statements are NOT correct as descriptions of what the auditor's understanding should include?
options: Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 4 only
questions.explanation: The source lists five items without qualification: applications used by the company, details of IT infrastructure components for each application, organisation structure and governance, the policies, procedures and processes followed, and IT risks and controls. Statements 1 and 3 correctly reflect items from that list, so they are not answers to a negative question. Statement 2 is not correct because organisation structure and governance appear expressly in the list; who owns and controls the IT function is part of the understanding, not something excluded as entity-level. Statement 4 is not correct because IT risks and controls are stated as a component of the understanding itself, whereas the question of whether automated controls will be relied upon is a later and different matter. The decisive point is that the source's list is unconditional and contains no reliance threshold.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question:
Situation P: The auditor records that purchase data passes through six applications of differing design before reaching the ledger, and notes the count as well as the design.
Situation Q: The auditor asks which of those six applications actually carry financial information through to the financial statements.
Situation R: The auditor lists the system credit-limit edit next to the sales manager's manual sanction note.
Situation S: The auditor notes that the warehouse uses drones for counting and the office uses biometric access control.
Area 1: Understand Flow of Transaction. Area 2: Identification of Significant Systems. Area 3: Identification of Manual and Automated Controls. Area 4: Identification of Technologies Used. Area 5: Assessing Complexity of IT Environment.

Which option correctly pairs each situation with the key consideration area it illustrates?
options: P-Area 2, Q-Area 1, R-Area 3, S-Area 4
P-Area 1, Q-Area 2, R-Area 5, S-Area 4
P-Area 1, Q-Area 2, R-Area 3, S-Area 4
P-Area 5, Q-Area 2, R-Area 3, S-Area 4
questions.explanation: Situation P is the flow-of-transaction area, which the source defines as identifying and understanding the nature and number of IT applications relevant to the flow of transactions; noting the count as well as the design is precisely that area. Situation Q is identification of significant systems, since the auditor is determining which applications matter as financial information flows to the statements. Situation R pairs a system edit with a human sanction, which is the manual and automated controls area whose identification is relevant to ROMM. Situation S is the technologies-used area, drones and biometrics being among the source's named examples of emerging technologies whose implementation must be understood and whose associated risks must be considered. The tempting error is P-Area 2, because counting applications overlaps in subject matter with identifying systems; the discriminator is that the flow area is defined by the nature and number of applications in the transaction flow, while the significant-systems area is defined by what carries financial information to the statements. Assigning R to complexity is likewise wrong, since complexity concerns the level of difficulty of individual characteristics rather than the type of control.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question: During the understanding phase, an auditor's note records that the entity has implemented a distributed ledger for inter-company settlement, robots on the packing line, a forecasting model, connected sensors in the cold store, fingerprint access at the warehouse door and an unmanned aircraft for roof inspection. Under the key consideration area 'Identification of Technologies Used', what is the auditor's obligation in respect of these technologies?
options: To document the names of such technologies, naming them being the whole of what this area requires.
To examine only those of them that produce figures appearing in the financial statements.
To understand the emerging technologies implemented and to consider whether there are risks arising from their use.
To evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of controls over each of them as a requirement of this area.
questions.explanation: The source states that there is a need to understand the emerging technologies implemented and to consider whether there are risks arising from their use, and it gives blockchain, robotics, artificial intelligence, internet of things, biometrics and drone as examples; the auditor's note therefore describes all six named examples and the obligation is the two-part one in option 2. Option 0 fails because the area requires consideration of risks as well as understanding, so a name list is not the whole requirement. Option 1 introduces a financial-statement filter that the source does not impose - the test is implementation and the risks from use, not visibility in the accounts. Option 4 misallocates the work: control identification belongs to the separate key area on manual and automated controls, and design and operating effectiveness evaluation is not what this area asks for. The decisive fact is the conjunction 'and consider whether there are risks arising from their use'.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question: In planning the audit of Varsha Appliances Ltd, an auditor proposes to assess the complexity of the IT environment once for the company, rating it 'moderate', and to apply that single rating identically to all eleven applications. Imagine that the only fact changed is that the eleven applications turn out to include a simple attendance logger with no interfaces on the one hand, and a self-configuring cloud finance module on the other. How does the conclusion on the proposed approach change, if at all?
options: It does not change, because the source makes complexity an attribute of the IT environment taken as a whole, so a single moderate rating properly summarises eleven applications.

It changes: since not all applications have the same level of complexity and the level for individual characteristics differs across applications, the single rating must be replaced by an application-wise assessment.
It changes only for the cloud finance module, because a simple attendance logger neither posts entries nor interfaces with any other application and is therefore outside the information system.
It does not change, because the auditor is entitled to rate every application at the highest level of complexity observed in the population in order to be prudent about the engagement.
questions.explanation: The source states two propositions under assessing complexity of the IT environment: not all applications have the same level of complexity, and the level of complexity for individual characteristics differs across applications. The changed fact makes both operative, because the two applications differ on the characteristics that drive complexity - one has no interfaces while the other configures itself - so an averaged 'moderate' rating conceals rather than records the position. Option 0 contradicts the first proposition outright. Option 2 is wrong in both directions: the attendance logger is an application used by the company and so is within the understanding, and the requirement is application-wise assessment rather than one exception. Option 3, which would rate everything at the worst observed complexity, substitutes prudence for assessment, since the source asks for the level of complexity of individual characteristics to be recognised rather than maximised. The decisive fact is the difference across applications in the level of complexity of individual characteristics.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question:
Case Study D. Aurika Pharmaceuticals Ltd operates in fourteen states. Its finance director reports that the company has implemented a distributed ledger for settlement with contract manufacturers, robots on the packaging lines, a system for batch-yield prediction, connected sensors in the cold chain, fingerprint access to the stores and an unmanned aircraft for inspecting terrace solar panels. In the planning memorandum the auditor enters these names in a schedule headed 'Emerging technologies' and closes the matter, reasoning that naming the technologies satisfies the requirement to understand the IT environment. He separately observes that the cold-chain sensor application is straightforward while the prediction model interacts with the inventory costing routine in ways he cannot summarise, and concludes that both therefore have the same complexity.

Statement 1: Closing the schedule after naming the technologies does not discharge the key area, because the auditor must also consider whether risks arise from their use.
Statement 2: All six technologies described in the case fall within the examples of emerging technologies named in the source.
Statement 3: The auditor's inability to summarise the prediction model is immaterial, since complexity is judged once for the environment as a whole.
Statement 4: Technologies that generate no journal entries are outside the identification of technologies used.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: Statements 1, 2, 3 and 4
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the source requires the auditor to understand the emerging technologies implemented and in addition to consider whether there are risks arising from their use, so a name list closes nothing. Statement 2 is correct, since blockchain, robotics, artificial intelligence, internet of things, biometrics and drone are precisely the six examples the source gives, and the case describes distributed ledger, robots, a predictive system, connected sensors, fingerprint access and an unmanned aircraft. Statement 3 is incorrect because the source says not all applications have the same level of complexity and that the level for individual characteristics differs across applications; the auditor's difficulty with the model relative to the sensors is the very evidence that the two differ. Statement 4 is incorrect, as the area is defined by implementation and by the risks from use, not by whether the technology itself posts entries - the sensors and robots plainly support recorded amounts even though they are not ledgers. The decisive fact is that the memorandum performs only the first half of one key area and asserts that the whole understanding is complete.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Key Areas of IT Environment
questions.question:
Case Study D. Aurika Pharmaceuticals Ltd operates in fourteen states. Its finance director reports that the company has implemented a distributed ledger for settlement with contract manufacturers, robots on the packaging lines, a system for batch-yield prediction, connected sensors in the cold chain, fingerprint access to the stores and an unmanned aircraft for inspecting terrace solar panels. In the planning memorandum the auditor enters these names in a schedule headed 'Emerging technologies' and closes the matter, reasoning that naming the technologies satisfies the requirement to understand the IT environment. He separately observes that the cold-chain sensor application is straightforward while the prediction model interacts with the inventory costing routine in ways he cannot summarise, and concludes that both therefore have the same complexity.

Action 1: Re-open the complexity assessment and evaluate the level of complexity of individual characteristics separately for the sensor application and for the prediction model.
Action 2: Consider, in respect of each implemented technology named, whether there are risks arising from its use.
Action 3: Identify both the manual checks operated by store supervisors and the automated elements built into the implemented systems, as relevant to identifying and assessing ROMM.
Action 4: Treat the naming schedule as a substitute for understanding the nature and number of IT applications relevant to the flow of transactions.

Which combination of actions is required by the source?
options: Actions 1, 2 and 3 only
Actions 1 and 4 only
Actions 2 and 4 only
Actions 4 only
questions.explanation: Action 1 responds to the source's statement that not all applications have the same level of complexity and that the level for individual characteristics differs across applications, which is exactly what the auditor ignored when he equated the two. Action 2 supplies the missing half of the technologies-used area, since the source requires the auditor to consider whether risks arise from the use of the implemented emerging technologies. Action 3 draws on the manual and automated controls area, the source stating that the entity's system of internal control contains both elements and that identification of both is relevant to the identification and assessment of ROMM. Action 4 is not permitted: understanding the flow of transactions is a distinct key area directed to the nature and number of IT applications relevant to that flow, and a schedule of technology names does not address either. The decisive fact is that three separate key areas were compressed into one naming exercise.

questions.question: Vardhman Logistics Ltd's digital-audit rollout report records four matters: (i) the automation tool was chosen by the IT team on technical grounds and the business benefit the organisation sought was left to be discovered after go-live; (ii) the affected staff were trained two weeks before go-live and their objections were minuted and answered; (iii) the dispatch process automated had already been documented and was identical across six hubs; (iv) no review has been made of who may change customer master data in the automated environment or of how the automated outputs are governed. Which of these matters remain inconsistent with the considerations and challenges the source sets out for a digital audit?
options: Matters (i) and (ii) only
Matters (i) and (iv) only
Matters (ii) and (iii) only
Matters (i), (iii) and (iv) only
questions.explanation: The source's considerations are to know what business benefit the organisation wants to achieve with automation, to think people first and not underestimate that change is difficult, to choose the right tool and automate the right process, to ensure the process works and is standardised before automating, and to reckon with challenges concerning data security and governance. Matter (i) offends the first consideration, since the business benefit was never established before the tool was selected. Matter (iv) engages the last, being a data security and governance gap over master data and automated outputs. Matters (ii) and (iii) satisfy the people-first consideration and the standardisation precondition respectively, so they are not open items and must not be selected in answer to a negative question. The decisive facts are the unanswered benefit question and the unreviewed access to master data, both of which the report treats as closed.

questions.category: Digital Audit - Meaning and Key Features
questions.question:
Statement 1: Among the key features is that a digital audit encourages the auditee to embrace the latest technological advancements and helps create a future for digital strategy and adopting new technologies.
Statement 2: A key feature is that it leads to savings in time and cost which can be utilised for more productive tasks.
Statement 3: A key feature is that it improves the quality of the opinion, leading to a more reliable audit report, and it can help the auditee make informed decisions.
Statement 4: A key feature is that the assessment of risks of material misstatement is taken over by the automated routines, human involvement being reduced to that extent.

Which of the above statements correctly reflect the key features of a digital audit as listed in the source?
options: Statements 1, 3 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
All of the statements
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 reproduce the five bullets the source lists under key features: embracing the latest technological advancements, creating a future for digital strategy and the adoption of new technologies, savings in time and cost usable for more productive tasks, improvement in the quality of the opinion leading to a more reliable audit report, and help to the auditee in making informed decisions. Statement 4 is not among them and is inconsistent with the source's own logic: improved risk assessment is described as an advantage under which management and auditors put their testing efforts on higher ROMM areas, and identification of manual and automated controls is stated as relevant to the auditor's identification and assessment of ROMM, so the assessment remains the auditor's. The distinction also matters for the meaning of a digital audit, which is placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems implemented - the systems are the subject of assurance, not the assessor. The decisive point is that automation of routine tasks is not automation of judgment.

questions.question: In an engagement annexure an audit firm writes: 'Our digital tools will cut the hours your staff spend producing routine schedules; and because the audit will be finished sooner, the overall cost of the audit may come down.' Which of the following most accurately maps these two claims to the advantages as the source states them?
options: Both claims fall under enhanced effectiveness and efficiency, since the source attributes the saving of time and cost to automated routine tasks in that advantage and nowhere else.

The first claim matches enhanced effectiveness and efficiency, arising from automated routine tasks saving time and cost; the second matches lower costs, arising because shortening the time to complete the audit may lower the audit's overall cost.
The first claim matches better analytics, which aids management and auditors in seeing trends and patterns; the second matches improved risk assessment, which directs effort to higher ROMM areas.

The first claim matches lower costs, arising because shortening the time to complete the audit may lower its overall cost; the second matches enhanced effectiveness and efficiency, arising because routine tasks are automated.
questions.explanation: The source lists enhanced effectiveness and efficiency with the explanation that automated routine task saves time and cost, and separately lists lower costs with the explanation that shortening the time to complete audit may lower the audit's overall cost. The first sentence of the annexure is about hours saved by automating a routine schedule, which is the efficiency advantage; the second is about fee consequence of a shorter engagement, which is the cost advantage. Option 0 collapses two distinct advantages into one and so loses the cause the source attaches to each. Option 2 substitutes advantages whose subject matter is trend information and risk-directed effort, neither of which the annexure mentions. Option 3 reverses the mapping, applying the cost explanation to the hours saved and the efficiency explanation to the shortened engagement. The decisive fact is that the source gives a different mechanism for each advantage, and the two mechanisms are not interchangeable.

questions.question:
Case Study E. Indus Tool Room Ltd is being audited under a digital audit approach for the first time. In the planning file the auditor records: (a) the applications in use, the IT infrastructure components behind each of them, the company's organisation structure and governance, the credit and accounting policies and procedures followed, and the IT risks and controls; (b) the significant applications, listed alongside his walk-through of how sales data reaches the general ledger; (c) the delivery-challan approval, which exists both as a system workflow step and as a signed paper document; and (d) a note stating that because (a) to (c) produced reliable information, the assess stage need not be performed.

Which of the following is the MOST appropriate evaluation of step (d)?
options: Step (d) is unobjectionable, because step (b) shows that the flow of transactions had not in fact been understood, and the whole file must therefore be re-performed before anything is assessed.
Step (d) is unobjectionable, since identifying both the manual workflow step and the signed paper document already amounts to identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement.

Step (d) is objectionable, because the source gives the stages of a digital audit as Understand - Identify - Assess, and assessment is a stage separate from the information gathering described in (a) to (c).
Step (d) is unobjectionable, because the object of a digital audit is assurance on the effectiveness of IT systems implemented, and the understanding recorded in (a) establishes that effectiveness.
questions.explanation: The source states that the stages involved in a digital audit are Understand, Identify and Assess. Steps (a) and (b) correspond to the understanding and identification stages, and step (c) to identifying the manual and automated elements of control, but none of them is the assess stage, so treating the third stage as spent is wrong on the face of the sequence. Option 0 and option 3 both reach the wrong conclusion for the wrong reason: option 0 asserts a defect in (b) that the case does not show, since identification of significant systems may be done concurrently with understanding the flow of financial information, while option 3 confuses the object of a digital audit with the completion of its stages, the recorded facts being inputs rather than an assessment. Option 1 is the strongest distractor because it exploits the source's link between control identification and ROMM, but identification and assessment of ROMM are what the identification stage feeds, not what substitutes for the assess stage of the digital audit. The decisive fact is the source's three-stage list, of which the third remains unperformed.

questions.category: Risks arising from use of IT
questions.question:
Vardhman Synthetics Limited ("VSL") manufactures at three plants and maintains its books on a single ERP instance. During system implementation VSL's IT team copied the approval hierarchy of the prior standalone purchase module into the ERP, and the team retained its own emergency administrator credential, described internally as "break-fix access", which is not logged and is used at the IT team's discretion. Five IT arrangements are relevant to the audit of the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025: (a) the ERP releases a purchase order only after the approving authority, fixed by value band in the workflow, has digitally approved it, and the order cannot be released without that approval; (b) the ERP applies the straight-line formula to the asset master, using cost and useful life captured at capitalisation, to compute monthly depreciation for posting to the statement of profit and loss; (c) VSL's treasury bank portal automatically pushes cleared daily transactions into the ERP cash ledger without any keying by VSL personnel; (d) the ERP generates an aged creditors report that the finance director reviews monthly before approving vendor statement reconciliations and that the audit team proposes to use for selecting confirmation balances; (e) the ERP permits a stores clerk to indenter a purchase order and, using the same user ID, to revise the delivery schedule of an order he himself had raised. VSL maintains a documented information security policy, and its annual access review is performed by the head of business operations but covers only 40 per cent of application users. VSL's change log shows that the ERP modification correcting a defective goods-reverse-capture screen was deployed directly by the IT team with no testing by any business user and with no entry in the change register, the entity having no procedure requiring that changes be tracked and recorded. Separately, the software vendor released a patch in October 2024 closing a critical vulnerability in the ERP, which VSL never deployed because no function owns the monitoring of vendor patch notifications. Data centre documentation at VSL covers physical entry, environmental controls and visitor registration.

Which of the following statements correctly matches an arrangement or control gap in VSL's environment with the specific risk arising from the use of IT to which it gives rise?
options: Fact (e) illustrates the risk of inappropriate manual intervention, because the stores clerk physically alters a delivery schedule.
The unlogged break-fix credential illustrates the risk of unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.
The October 2024 patch which VSL never deployed illustrates the risk of failure to make necessary update to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.
The copying of the prior approval hierarchy from the legacy module without any business verification illustrates the risk of data loss or data corruption of the purchase ledger.
questions.explanation: The source lists, as a risk arising from the use of IT, failure to make necessary update to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment, and a vendor patch closing a critical vulnerability that is never deployed is exactly that failure, because the environment has not been brought into the state it requires. The decisive fact is that nothing was changed, so the exposure is the omission rather than an unauthorised act. Option (a) mislabels fact (e), which concerns a person exercising two incompatible functions and therefore touches access and segregation of duties rather than intervention in an automated process. Option (b) is wrong because break-fix access enables changes to data and gives rise to the separate risk of IT personnel gaining extra access, not to modification of the application. Option (d) attaches loss or corruption of data to a configuration copied without verification, which is not a data integrity failure.

questions.category: Risks arising from use of IT
questions.question:
Meridian Retail Limited ("MRL") operates 240 stores on a point-of-sale ("POS") application that posts daily sales summaries to a central finance system. Four facts emerge during the audit of the year ended 31 March 2025. (1) The finance team prepares the monthly gross-margin analytical review exclusively from the POS system-generated category-wise sales report. (2) The finance system applies the configured scheme to compute employee provident fund and depreciation for posting, instead of the accounting staff performing these computations. (3) A user audit performed by the IT support desk shows that the support team held administrator rights on both the POS and finance systems, and that no business management approval of such access had ever been obtained and no review had ever been performed outside the IT function. (4) Two months before the year end a power event at the hosted data centre made the previous nine days of posted transactions unavailable, and the entries had to be reconstructed from POS records. MRL maintains security policies and procedures and a change management policy, both current and reviewed annually; no change has been made to any of MRL's systems during the year and the change management policy has accordingly never been invoked. MRL has no procedure covering the backup of production systems and no test has ever been performed to establish whether data can be recovered.

Which combination of risks arising from the use of IT is directly evidenced by the facts of MRL's environment?
options: Inappropriate manual intervention together with data loss or data corruption.
Possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access together with data loss or data corruption.
Unauthorised access to data or improper changes to data, together with the possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access.
Failure to make necessary update to IT applications, together with inappropriate manual intervention.
questions.explanation: Fact (3) evidences the possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access in the precise form the source lists it: administrator rights on both the POS and finance systems were held by the support desk with no approval by business management and no review outside IT. Fact (4), in which a power event made nine days of posted transactions unavailable and the entries had to be reconstructed, evidences the separate listed risk of data loss. The decisive facts are therefore unapproved and unreviewed IT privilege and unrecoverable production data. Options (a) and (d) invoke inappropriate manual intervention, which the source reserves for a person interfering with a process the IT environment is designed to perform, not for staff preparing their own review; option (c) files fact (3) under general unauthorised access to data, although no data was reached or altered without authorisation.

questions.category: Risks arising from use of IT
questions.question: A payments application of a listed entity exhibits the four situations set out below. Which situation is NOT one of the risks arising from the use of IT identified in the source list?
options: A database administrator obtains the ability to alter posted vendor bank details while performing routine maintenance.
A developer modifies the interest computation routine of the loan application and moves it into production without the change being recorded.
A power interruption at the hosted data centre leaves the day's posted transactions unavailable.
An accounts executive recalculates a system-produced ageing report in a spreadsheet before the finance controller reviews it.
questions.explanation: The source list covers unauthorised access to data or improper changes to data, the possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access, unauthorised changes to data, unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment, failure to make necessary update to those applications or aspects, inappropriate manual intervention, and data loss or data corruption. Situations (a), (b) and (c) fall within that list as IT personnel gaining extra access, unauthorised changes to the IT application, and data loss respectively. Situation (d) does not, because a person performing by hand a computation that the system never performed is not a person intervening inappropriately in an automated process. The decisive question is whether the human act replaced, defeated or overrode a function the IT environment was designed to perform.

questions.category: Risks arising from use of IT
questions.question: A statutory auditor is assessing a textile entity that migrated to a single ERP. Which conclusion about the applicable risk arising from the use of IT is MOST appropriate?
options: Because the ERP has not been modified since implementation, the entity is not exposed to the risk of unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.

Because the vendor released a critical patch that the entity's IT function never applied, the entity is exposed to the risk of failure to make necessary update to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.
Because the ERP computes depreciation each month without any human involvement at all, the entity is exposed to the risk of inappropriate manual intervention.
Because two data-entry users in the sales section share one login and password, the entity is exposed to the risk of data loss or data corruption.
questions.explanation: The source treats failure to make necessary update to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment as an independent risk, and an unapplied critical patch is such a failure, so conclusion (b) stands on its own terms. Conclusion (a) confuses occurrence with exposure: the absence of changes to date does not remove the risk that such changes may be made. Conclusion (c) inverts the concept, because a computation performed by the system instead of a person removes manual intervention rather than creating it. Conclusion (d) attaches the wrong consequence to the fact, since a shared login bears on authorised access and separation of roles, whereas data loss or corruption concerns the integrity and availability of the data itself.

questions.category: Risks arising from use of IT
questions.question:
Kaveri Agro Processing Limited implemented an integrated ERP on 1 April 2024. The procurement module releases a purchase order only after workflow approval at the value band configured for the approving authority. The asset module computes depreciation using the straight-line formula configured in the asset master. The warehouse module pushes despatch advice data into the freight partner's billing system through programmed logic, and freight charges are accounted in the ERP from that feed. A bank feed brings loan-portal transaction data into the ERP loan schedule. The finance head prepares a monthly vendor-wise purchase summary from system reports, uses the summary to select vendors for balance confirmation, and compares it with the purchase register as an analytical procedure. The ERP is configured so that the user who creates a vendor master record cannot be the same user who releases a payment against that vendor. In December 2024 the vendor released a critical patch closing a security vulnerability in the ERP, which the IT function never deployed because nobody owns the monitoring of patch notifications. In January 2025 the IT department moved an untested ERP update containing new tax accrual logic into production. The IT team holds an unlogged emergency credential capable of altering both configuration and posted data, and the entity has no procedure requiring that IT changes be tracked and recorded.

Which of the following statements is INCORRECT in matching a matter in Kaveri's environment with the risk arising from the use of IT that it evidences?
options: The ability of the IT team's emergency credential to modify posted data evidences the risk of the possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access.

The absence of any procedure requiring that IT changes be tracked and recorded, taken with the untested January 2025 update, evidences the risk of unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.
The existence of the despatch advice interface and of the bank feed evidences the risk of unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.
The absence of any backup or recovery procedure for the ERP database evidences the risk of data loss or data corruption.
questions.explanation: Interfaces are defined by the source as programmed logic that transfer data from one IT system to another, and the mere operation of such logic evidences a dependency, not a risk of unauthorised changes to the application or environment, so the third statement is the incorrect one. The other three each pair a genuine exposure with a risk the source lists: an emergency credential held by IT that can modify posted data, an untested and untracked change moved into production, and the absence of recoverability. The decisive point is that a risk must be matched with a failure or exposure and not with the presence of an IT arrangement, and the December 2024 patch that was never deployed would have been the correct fact for the change-related risk if the statement had been framed that way. A candidate who reasons that data moving between systems is automatically a change risk has confused the interface dependency with the risk arising from it.

questions.category: Risks arising from use of IT
questions.question:
Daksh Infra Limited ("DIL") operates an ERP for construction contracts. In August 2024 DIL's IT department, while resolving a performance complaint, modified the logic that determines the work-in-progress cost pool; the modification was released to production on the same day with no testing by the contracts or finance function. In January 2025 the IT department granted an external consultant permanent access to the production contract cost tables so that a report could be prepared on one occasion. Neither event was reported to management as an IT matter. The statutory auditor of DIL identifies that the ERP is used to record and process contract cost data for inclusion in the financial statements and therefore intends to rely on general IT controls.

Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate conclusion about the risks arising from the use of IT in DIL's environment?
options: No risk arising from the use of IT is present in respect of the work-in-progress cost pool, because the IT department modified the logic in good faith to resolve a performance complaint.
The untested modification of the logic determining the work-in-progress cost pool engages the risk of unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment.
The permanent grant of access to production contract cost tables engages the risk of unauthorised access to data or improper changes to data.
The fact that the IT department could make both changes without reporting them to management engages the risk of the possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access.
questions.explanation: The source's list of risks arising from the use of IT is framed by what may happen to the application, the environment and the data, and nowhere conditions a risk on the motive of the person who made the change, so the first conclusion is the least appropriate. The modification of cost-determining logic without testing is squarely within the risk of unauthorised changes to IT applications or other aspects of the IT environment, and permanent access to production cost tables for a one-off report is within the risk of unauthorised access to data or improper changes to data. The absence of any management visibility of either act is what the source describes as the possibility of IT personnel gaining extra access. The decisive fact for the incorrect conclusion is that good intention does not cure an uncontrolled change, because the financial data for inclusion in the financial statements is produced by logic that no one has verified.

questions.question: A retail entity's environment contains the four arrangements below. On the source's definition of when an IT dependency is created, which arrangement does NOT create an IT dependency?
