(iv) A storekeeper received a telephone call from a person claiming to be from a reputed insurance company and, being told that his claim would otherwise lapse, disclosed his bank account details.

What changes if the deception in (i) is re-cast so that the fabricated sender identity is used in a text message sent to the chief financial officer, asking him to reveal the net-banking password needed to release the vendor advance?
options: Nothing changes: email spoofing, phishing and whaling all continue to apply exactly as before, since only the delivery instrument has been altered and not the identity of the target or the object of the message.
Whaling ceases to apply because it required an email channel; email spoofing and smishing continue to apply.
Phishing ceases to apply, because the source confines its enticement language to individuals rather than to officers of the entity who hold net-banking access.
Email spoofing alone ceases, since its description turns on emails with forged sender addresses; phishing through the SMS channel, as smishing, and whaling both continue to apply.
questions.explanation: Only the delivery instrument has been altered; the target and the objective are untouched. Email spoofing is defined by the source as a cyberattack which targets businesses by using emails with forged sender addresses, so once the email is removed that description has nothing to attach to, and domain spoofing is equally unavailable because no fake website or domain is used. Phishing expressly lists SMS among its channels, so the parent description survives, and smishing, whose stated object is to induce individuals to reveal personal information through text messages pretending from reputable companies, is the closest sub-type. Whaling is defined by the seniority of the target and by the purpose of stealing money or information, neither of which depends on the channel, so it survives unchanged. The answer which treats everything as unchanged overlooks the email element of email spoofing; the answer which drops whaling wrongly makes it channel-based; and the answer which drops phishing contradicts the channel list in the definition.

questions.question:
Case: Orbit Payments Ltd operates a payment gateway. On 4 November 2025, between 21:00 and 23:30, merchant users could not log in to their online accounts and merchant support email could not be retrieved. Network logs showed the gateway's public address being flooded with a very large volume of fabricated requests arriving from a large number of machines. No record in the settlement ledger was added, changed, removed or made visible, and no demand for money was received. In his month-end note the head of IT recorded that the entity "had suffered a ransomware attack because staff were unable to perform routine tasks", while the entity's unaudited press note attributed the same episode to the site having exceeded its own designed server capacity. M/s Kulkarni & Associates, the statutory auditors, are evaluating these two classifications.

Which of the following statements are correct in evaluating the two classifications put forward by management?
Statement 1: The episode fits the description of a Denial-of-Service attack, which is a malicious, targeted attack that floods a network with false requests to disrupt business operations.
Statement 2: The press note is consistent with the source, because a flood of requests which exceeds capacity is a Denial-of-Service attack whether or not it was malicious or targeted.
Statement 3: The head of IT's note is not supported, because ransomware requires the adversary to encrypt the victim's data and to offer the decryption key in exchange for payment.
Statement 4: The note is correct, because inability of users to perform routine tasks such as accessing email, websites or online accounts is stated as a consequence of ransomware.
options: Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The logs show a very large volume of fabricated requests directed at the gateway's public address with the object of disruption, which is the mechanism the source attributes to a Denial-of-Service attack, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 3 is correct because none of the ransomware elements is present, nothing in the settlement ledger having been encrypted and no key having been offered for payment. Statement 2 fails because the source's description is expressly of a malicious, targeted attack, so an unplanned breach of designed capacity is not brought within it and the press note cannot claim support from that description. Statement 4 reverses the source, since the inability of users to perform routine tasks such as accessing email, websites or online accounts is given as the consequence of a Denial-of-Service attack, which is the very fact that makes the outage evidence of DoS rather than of ransomware; the combinations admitting either statement 2 or statement 4 therefore fail.

questions.question:
Case: Orbit Payments Ltd operates a payment gateway. On 4 November 2025, between 21:00 and 23:30, merchant users could not log in to their online accounts and merchant support email could not be retrieved. Network logs showed the gateway's public address being flooded with a very large volume of fabricated requests arriving from a large number of machines. No record in the settlement ledger was added, changed, removed or made visible, and no demand for money was received. In his month-end note the head of IT recorded that the entity "had suffered a ransomware attack because staff were unable to perform routine tasks", while the entity's unaudited press note attributed the same episode to the site having exceeded its own designed server capacity. M/s Kulkarni & Associates, the statutory auditors, are evaluating these two classifications.

Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion for the auditors on the competing classifications?
options: The episode is a ransomware attack, because disruption of routine tasks is a consequence the source records for ransomware as well as for a denial-of-service attack, so either label may be used.
The episode is email spoofing, because merchant support email was among the services which failed during the two and a half hours.
The episode is a Denial-of-Service attack, the malicious flood of false requests supplying the mechanism and the outage of email, websites and online accounts supplying the stated consequence.
The episode need not be classified at all, because the definition of a cyber-attack requires data to have been damaged, stolen or destroyed rather than merely disabled or altered.
questions.explanation: The source's Denial-of-Service description has two limbs, the mechanism of a malicious, targeted flood of a network with false requests to disrupt business operations and the consequence of users being unable to perform routine tasks such as accessing email, websites or online accounts, and both limbs are satisfied on these facts. The ransomware label cannot be preferred merely because work was disrupted, since that description requires the adversary to encrypt the victim's data and to offer the decryption key in exchange for payment, and a disruption without encryption or a payment demand is not ransomware. Email spoofing requires emails with forged sender addresses aimed at a business, and the mere unavailability of a mail service is not that. The last answer is wrong on the definition of a cyber-attack, whose enumerated intents are alternatives and include disabling and altering data, and in any event none of them needs to be executed for an attempt to fall within the definition.

questions.category: Cyber Risks – Malware and DoS together
questions.question:
Case: Orbit Payments Ltd operates a payment gateway. On 4 November 2025, between 21:00 and 23:30, merchant users could not log in to their online accounts and merchant support email could not be retrieved. Network logs showed the gateway's public address being flooded with a very large volume of fabricated requests arriving from a large number of machines. No record in the settlement ledger was added, changed, removed or made visible, and no demand for money was received. In his month-end note the head of IT recorded that the entity "had suffered a ransomware attack because staff were unable to perform routine tasks", while the entity's unaudited press note attributed the same episode to the site having exceeded its own designed server capacity. M/s Kulkarni & Associates, the statutory auditors, are evaluating these two classifications.

What changes if, alongside the flood of fabricated requests, the intruder also encrypts the merchant settlement records and leaves a screen demanding payment in exchange for the key, while the flood continues?
options: The episode becomes ransomware only, because the source sets out the common types of cyber-attack as alternatives for a single episode, so the later and more serious description displaces the earlier one.
Two descriptions now apply together, ransomware as a subset of malware for the encryption with the key offered for payment, and Denial-of-Service for the continuing flood.
The ransomware element ceases to be a subset of malware and becomes a sub-type of phishing, because the payment demand is addressed to users.
Only the Denial-of-Service description continues to apply, because ransomware additionally requires the victim's data to be destroyed as well as encrypted.
questions.explanation: The source presents ransomware as one of four subsets of malware, and malware, denial-of-service attacks, phishing and spoofing as separate common types of cyber-attack, so an episode which satisfies two descriptions is classified under both rather than under one to the exclusion of the other. The added facts supply exactly the ransomware elements, the adversary encrypting the victim's data and offering the decryption key in exchange for payment, while the unchanged facts continue to supply the Denial-of-Service elements. Treating the two labels as mutually exclusive reads an exclusivity into the list which the source does not state. Moving ransomware into phishing's sub-types confuses the levels of the taxonomy, since those sub-types are spear phishing, whaling, smishing and vishing. Requiring destruction of the data as well as encryption borrows an intent from the definition of a cyber-attack and imposes it on the ransomware description, which speaks only of encryption and payment.

questions.question:
Case: Trellis Retail Ltd equips 400 field sales persons with company-owned smartphones. During 2025-26 three events were reported to the auditors.
(x) A "free coupon scanner" obtained from a third-party app store acted as advertised but also copied the address book and the text messages from the phones to an external address.
(y) The same campaign had been preceded by text messages, sent in the name of a reputed e-commerce platform, asking sales persons to share their personal details to claim a recharge benefit.
(z) The entity's own mobile-device-management console, operated by the IT team under authority, wiped the handset of an employee who had resigned without returning it.

Which of the following statements are correct?
Statement 1: Event (x) answers to the description of mobile malware and also to that of a Trojan, since it is malware designed to target mobile devices and it appeared as legitimate software disguised as a harmless free download.
Statement 2: The two labels in statement 1 are compatible, because the source presents ransomware, fileless malware, Trojan and mobile malware as subsets of malware rather than as mutually exclusive categories.
Statement 3: Event (y) is smishing, being text messages pretending from a reputable company sent to induce individuals to reveal personal information.
Statement 4: Event (z) is mobile malware, because data on a mobile device was destroyed.
options: Statements 1 and 4 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Malware is any program or code created with intent to do harm to a computer, network or server, and its listed subsets describe different features of the same malicious program, namely what it disguises itself as, how it executes and what platform it targets, so a mobile-targeting program delivered as a harmless free download legitimately carries both descriptions and statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is correct on both elements of smishing, the text-message instrument and the pretended reputable sender, with the stated object of drawing out personal information. Statement 4 fails because the wiping was performed by the entity's own authorised management console acting under authority, whereas malware requires a program or code created with intent to do harm, so authorised internal administration is not malicious software merely because it deleted mobile data. Each of the three other combinations includes statement 4 and therefore cannot stand.

questions.question:
Case: Trellis Retail Ltd equips 400 field sales persons with company-owned smartphones. During 2025-26 three events were reported to the auditors.
(x) A "free coupon scanner" obtained from a third-party app store acted as advertised but also copied the address book and the text messages from the phones to an external address.
(y) The same campaign had been preceded by text messages, sent in the name of a reputed e-commerce platform, asking sales persons to share their personal details to claim a recharge benefit.
(z) The entity's own mobile-device-management console, operated by the IT team under authority, wiped the handset of an employee who had resigned without returning it.

On event (x) a junior team member objects that describing the coupon scanner as both mobile malware and a Trojan is self-contradictory, and that one of the two labels must be dropped. Which response to that objection is most appropriate?
options: The objection is well founded; the four subsets of malware are mutually exclusive categories, and where more than one appears to fit, only the description matching the device actually targeted should be retained.
The objection is well founded; the single correct label is whaling, since the sales persons were enticed into installing the scanner by a free offer.

The objection is not well founded; the subsets describe different features of one program, and here the decisive facts are that it targeted mobile devices and presented itself as a harmless free download.
The objection is not well founded; the scanner is better described as fileless malware, because malicious activity on a handset need not leave a file which the user can see.
questions.explanation: Ransomware, fileless malware, Trojan and mobile malware are given as subsets of malware, not as alternatives at the same level, so an item of malicious code can satisfy the description of more than one subset without contradiction. On these facts the program targeted mobile devices, which is the whole content of the mobile-malware description, and it appeared as legitimate software disguised as a harmless free download, which is the whole content of the Trojan description, so both labels must be preserved. Insisting on exclusivity asserts a feature the source does not state. Substituting whaling moves the item into an entirely different family, since whaling is a sub-type of phishing defined by targeting senior employees to steal money or information, and neither element is present for 400 field sales persons. Substituting fileless malware is the technical trap, because that description turns on the use of legitimate tools built into the system, whereas the scanner was itself the malicious program installed from an app store.

questions.question:
Case: Kalinga Traders Ltd, an importer, is being audited by M/s Patnaik & Co. Two deceptions were reported.
(P) A freight forwarder received an email which displayed, as its sender, the address of the company's purchase manager with whom the forwarder regularly corresponded; that address had in fact been fabricated. The email asked the forwarder to re-confirm the bank details in its records.
(Q) A vendor was directed to a login page at "kalingatraders-portal.com", which reproduced the appearance of the company's genuine supplier portal, and there entered its username and password.
For the month's vendor-payment testing the auditors also noted that a payment had been released by the accounts team after an instruction which arrived as a voicemail from a number displayed as that of a reputed logistics company.

Which of the following statements are correct as to the concepts the facts support?
Statement 1: (P) is email spoofing, being an attack which targets a business by using emails with forged sender addresses.
Statement 2: (Q) is domain spoofing, which the source places among the types of spoofing while also describing it as a form of phishing in which a known business is impersonated through a fake website or domain in order to be trusted.
Statement 3: (Q) independently satisfies the description of phishing, because the vendor was enticed to share sensitive information, namely its password.
Statement 4: The voicemail instruction falls outside the source's description of phishing, because that description is confined to email, SMS and social media.
options: Statements 1 and 4 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The fabricated sender address in (P) is the single distinguishing feature the source gives for email spoofing, and the target is a business, so statement 1 is correct. Statements 2 and 3 are both correct and are not in conflict, since the source's own wording calls domain spoofing a form of phishing, and the parent phishing description is separately satisfied because the imitation portal drew out a password. Statement 4 is wrong because the channels named in the phishing description are email, SMS, phone and social media, so a call or voice message is inside the family, and where the channel is a call or voice message pretending from a reputable source the relevant sub-type is vishing; the combinations which rely on statement 4, and the combination which omits statement 3, are therefore unsupportable.

questions.question:
Case: Kalinga Traders Ltd, an importer, is being audited by M/s Patnaik & Co. Two deceptions were reported.
(P) A freight forwarder received an email which displayed, as its sender, the address of the company's purchase manager with whom the forwarder regularly corresponded; that address had in fact been fabricated. The email asked the forwarder to re-confirm the bank details in its records.
(Q) A vendor was directed to a login page at "kalingatraders-portal.com", which reproduced the appearance of the company's genuine supplier portal, and there entered its username and password.
For the month's vendor-payment testing the auditors also noted that a payment had been released by the accounts team after an instruction which arrived as a voicemail from a number displayed as that of a reputed logistics company.

What changes if, in (Q), the vendor had been sent a link to the company's genuine supplier portal, while the covering email continued to display the fabricated address of the purchase manager?
options: Nothing changes: any attack which reaches a victim through a link to a website is domain spoofing, whatever the email said.
Email spoofing ceases to apply, because the vendor was not asked to reveal anything on a fake page.
Domain spoofing ceases to apply, because the site reached is the company's genuine one, while email spoofing continues to apply because the sender address of the covering email remains forged.
Both domain spoofing and email spoofing cease to apply, because neither can be made out without a demand for payment, and only the general concept of a Denial-of-Service attack survives.
questions.explanation: Domain spoofing is defined by the impersonation of a known business through a fake website or domain in order to fool people into trusting the attacker; remove the imitation address and that description has no factual support, however convincing the covering email remained. Email spoofing, by contrast, is defined solely by the use of emails with forged sender addresses to target businesses, and that fact is preserved in the modified version, so this label survives, as does the general spoofing concept of disguising the cybercriminal as a known or trusted source. Treating any link as domain spoofing confuses the medium with the impersonated object. Transferring the fake-page requirement into email spoofing adds a condition the source does not impose. Retaining a Denial-of-Service attack introduces a flood of false requests to disrupt business operations, which is nowhere alleged.

questions.question:
Case: Kalinga Traders Ltd, an importer, is being audited by M/s Patnaik & Co. Two deceptions were reported.
(P) A freight forwarder received an email which displayed, as its sender, the address of the company's purchase manager with whom the forwarder regularly corresponded; that address had in fact been fabricated. The email asked the forwarder to re-confirm the bank details in its records.
(Q) A vendor was directed to a login page at "kalingatraders-portal.com", which reproduced the appearance of the company's genuine supplier portal, and there entered its username and password.
For the month's vendor-payment testing the auditors also noted that a payment had been released by the accounts team after an instruction which arrived as a voicemail from a number displayed as that of a reputed logistics company.

Which one of the following statements about the concepts illustrated by this case is NOT correct?
options: Spoofing is described as a technique through which a cybercriminal disguises himself as a known or trusted source, the adversary thereby being able to access targeted devices for stealing information.
Domain spoofing and email spoofing are the two types of spoofing given in the source, and the former is additionally described as a form of phishing.
Phishing is confined in the source to attacks on senior employees, so (P) and (Q) would have to be reclassified as whaling.
The distinguishing feature given for email spoofing is the forged sender address, whereas that given for domain spoofing is the impersonation of a known business through a fake website or domain.
questions.explanation: Whaling is the sub-type defined by targeting senior employees for money or information; the parent phishing description is not so confined, since it covers email, SMS, phone and social media used to entice any victim to share sensitive information or to download a malicious file. The forwarder, the vendor and the accounts team here are not described as senior employees, so confining phishing to whaling would leave (P) and (Q) unclassified, which is what makes this the incorrect statement. The remaining statements are all supported: the general spoofing description of disguising the attacker as a known or trusted source in order to reach targeted devices, the two listed types of spoofing together with the cross-reference calling domain spoofing a form of phishing, and the single distinguishing feature which separates forged sender addresses from fake websites or domains. A candidate who reads "targeting businesses" in the email-spoofing description as meaning "targeting senior management" is the intended victim of this question.

questions.question:
Case: While auditing Meridian Steel Ltd for 2025-26, the auditor reads three entries in the entity's incident register.
Entry 1: "The accounts workstation's ledger folder was encrypted by an intruder; a message on the screen offered the key against payment of ₹ 4 lakh."
Entry 2: "No program was added to the mail server; commands were run through the scripting utility supplied with the operating system."
Entry 3: "An email to the accounts desk displayed the fabricated address of a known supplier and asked for its bank details to be re-confirmed."
Which one of the following combinations classifies all three entries correctly?
options: Entry 1 - Denial-of-Service attack; Entry 2 - Trojan; Entry 3 - Whaling
Entry 1 - Ransomware; Entry 2 - Trojan; Entry 3 - Domain spoofing
Entry 1 - Fileless malware; Entry 2 - Mobile malware; Entry 3 - Spear phishing
Entry 1 - Ransomware; Entry 2 - Fileless malware; Entry 3 - Email spoofing
questions.explanation: Ransomware is the adversary encrypting the victim's data and offering the decryption key in exchange for payment, and Entry 1 contains both elements. Fileless malware is malicious activity which uses legitimate tools built into the system to execute a cyber-attack, and Entry 2 states expressly that no program was added and the built-in scripting utility was used; a Trojan by contrast requires malware appearing to be legitimate software disguised as harmless files such as free downloads, and no such file exists. Email spoofing is a cyberattack which targets businesses by using emails with forged sender addresses, which is exactly Entry 3. Domain spoofing is unavailable for Entry 3 because no fake website or domain was used, whaling is unavailable because no senior employee was targeted, and mobile malware is unavailable because a mail server is not a mobile device. Reading Entry 1 as a Denial-of-Service attack also fails, since nothing was flooded with false requests and users were not prevented from performing routine tasks.

questions.question:
Case: An assistant in the accounts section of Ranga Jewellers Ltd received a telephone call, followed by a voice message, from a person identifying himself as the relationship manager of the entity's banking company and asking for the assistant's internet-banking password to "stay a fraudulent debit". The assistant read out the password. No text message and no email was involved, and nothing was downloaded on to any device.
Which one of the following is the MOST specific description given in the source?
options: Smishing
Whaling
Vishing
Trojan
questions.explanation: Vishing, or voice phishing, is described as the fraudulent use of calls and voice messages pretending from reputable companies to convince individuals to reveal private information, and both the instrument and the pretended banking source match that description exactly. Smishing requires the text-message channel, which the case rules out. Whaling requires that the attack specifically target senior employees to steal money or information, and an assistant in the accounts section is not so described, notwithstanding that a bank official was impersonated. A Trojan requires malicious software appearing as legitimate software disguised as harmless files such as free downloads, and no software was delivered here at all.

questions.question:
Case: Three employees of Nirmal Mills Ltd received, on their personal social-media accounts, messages in the name of a reputed logistics company inviting them to download a "free proof-of-delivery viewer"; the program installed a virus on their phones. A fourth employee received an identical message on the entity's internal staff chat tool, which the source does not mention among the channels, and deleted it unread.
Which of the following statements are correct?
Statement 1: The social-media messages fall within the source's description of phishing, because social media is a listed channel and the enticement extends to downloading a malicious file that will install viruses on the computer or phone.
Statement 2: Because the phones were the infected devices, the incident can be described only as smishing.
Statement 3: The program itself falls within the malware description, and its presentation as a free viewer fits the Trojan description.
Statement 4: The internal chat message is vishing, because it arrived on an electronic channel other than email.
options: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 4 only
Statements 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The phishing description supplies both elements needed by statement 1: the channel list includes social media, and the two permitted objects are enticing a victim to share sensitive information such as passwords or to download a malicious file that will install viruses on the computer or phone. Statement 3 is correct because malware is any program or code created with intent to do harm to a computer, network or server, and a program which appears to be legitimate software disguised as a harmless free download answers the Trojan description. Statement 2 fails because smishing is defined by the text-message channel, not by the type of device ultimately infected. Statement 4 fails because vishing requires calls and voice messages, and the source's channel list does not extend to an internal chat tool, which is why the fourth employee's message is left without a channel-based sub-type rather than being re-labelled.

questions.question:
Case: The forensic report on Vayu Airlines Ltd reads: "The intruder placed no new program on the mail server. All activity was carried out through the command utilities that come with the operating system, and traces of the intrusion were present only in memory." The head of IT nonetheless reports to the board that this was "a Trojan, because the intruder entered through a legitimate-looking route".
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate evaluation of the two descriptions?
options: The head of IT is right, because anything which travels through a legitimate-looking route is for that reason alone a Trojan under the source, whatever was or was not placed on the server.
The forensic report describes a Denial-of-Service attack, because abnormal activity was observed on a server which holds mail for the whole entity.
The two descriptions are equivalent, because fileless malware is simply the name the source gives to a Trojan designed to escape detection by running inside the system rather than as a file on it.

The forensic report describes fileless malware, since the source defines it as malicious activity using legitimate tools built into the system, whereas a Trojan requires malware disguised as a harmless file.
questions.explanation: The distinguishing fact is the mechanism: nothing was written to disk and the operating system's own command utilities were used, which is verbatim the description of fileless malware. The Trojan description turns on the disguise of malicious software as a harmless file offered, for example, as a free download; the report expressly states that no new program was placed on the server, so the disguise element is absent and the head of IT has substituted a loose sense of "legitimate-looking" for the source's sense of a file which looks like harmless software. Treating the two as equivalent assumes that one is a detection-evasion name for the other, but the source lists them as separate subsets with different defining features and says nothing about escaping detection. Bringing in a Denial-of-Service attack requires a flood of false requests and the prevention of routine tasks, neither of which is reported, and generalising the "legitimate route" idea would swallow every subset.

questions.category: Cyber Risks – Malware and phishing: labelling exercise
questions.question: Four entries are transcribed below from an entity's incident register together with the labels the entity attached to them. Which one of those labels is NOT supported by the descriptions given in the source?
options: "The attacker ran malicious commands through the backup utility supplied with the server, without adding any file" - labelled Fileless malware.
"The attacker encrypted the design library and asked for payment before releasing the key" - labelled Ransomware.
"A no-cost screen recorder obtained from a website was found to have opened a hidden administrative account" - labelled Trojan.
"A recorded telephone message in the name of the entity's insurer asked a clerk to disclose his policy and bank details" - labelled Smishing.
questions.explanation: Smishing is confined by the source to text messages pretending from reputable companies, whereas the fraudulent use of calls and voice messages pretending from reputable companies to convince individuals to reveal private information is vishing; the instrument here is a recorded telephone message, so the register's label is unsupported even though the pretended source was an insurer and the object was disclosure of personal information. The other three labels each match the single defining feature in the source: fileless malware uses legitimate tools built into the system to execute a cyber-attack; ransomware encrypts the victim's data and offers the decryption key in exchange for payment; a Trojan is malware appearing to be legitimate software disguised as harmless files like free downloads, which is what a no-cost screen recorder obtained from a website is. Treating "text pretending from a reputable company" and "voice message pretending from a reputable company" as interchangeable is the error this question tests.

questions.question:
Case: An engineer at Prism Design Ltd configured the entity's own document-encryption product to lock all active drawings over a weekend, with the keys held by the IT department, and the drawings were released on Monday morning. Separately, on 12 September, the same folder was found locked with a message demanding payment to a foreign wallet in exchange for the key. The head of IT reported both episodes to the auditors as "two ransomware attacks".
Which of the following is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: Only the September episode is ransomware, because the description requires an adversary to encrypt the data and to offer the key for payment, while the weekend episode was authorised internal use of the entity's own tool.
Both episodes are ransomware, because in each the data was encrypted and could be restored only with a key, and that is the practical test which this sub-type is meant to supply.
Neither episode is ransomware, because in neither was any data destroyed or exposed to persons outside the entity.

Only the weekend episode is ransomware, because keeping the keys inside the organisation is in substance an offer of decryption, the payment element being satisfied by the users' loss of access to their own drawings.
questions.explanation: The ransomware description has three components, an adversary, encryption of the victim's data and the offer of the decryption key in exchange for payment, and the September episode supplies all three while the weekend episode supplies only the middle one. Encryption carried out by the entity's own staff under authority, using the entity's own product, with keys retained internally and release scheduled in advance, is an administrative act rather than a cyber-attack, since a cyber-attack is an attempt to gain unauthorized access with one of the enumerated harmful intents. Reading the technical symptom as the classification is the error in the second conclusion, and the fourth inverts the requirement of an adversary by treating internal key custody as a costless version of the offer. The third conclusion is also wrong, because the definition of a cyber-attack lists disabling and altering as alternative intents, so neither destruction nor exposure is necessary for the September episode to qualify.

questions.question:
Case: Zenith Bazaar Ltd's customer website was unavailable for 40 minutes during a flash sale. Two explanations were debated, that the site had exceeded its designed capacity, or that it had been the target of a malicious flood of fabricated requests. The auditors will record the type of cyber-attack only if the second explanation is established.
Which additional fact, standing alone, is decisive under the source's description of a Denial-of-Service attack?
options: That customers were unable to perform routine tasks such as accessing the website, their online accounts and the support email of the entity throughout the 40 minutes of the outage.
That the traffic reaching the site consisted of false requests directed at the network so as to disrupt business operations, and that the attack was malicious and targeted.
That no customer record was altered, removed or made visible at any point during the outage.
That the entity's own capacity monitor had warned of an approaching limit at almost the same time as the sale opened.
questions.explanation: The element which distinguishes a Denial-of-Service attack from an ordinary overload in the source's description is that it is a malicious, targeted attack which floods a network with false requests in order to disrupt business operations, so only that fact settles the question. Customer inability to access the website, online accounts and email is the stated consequence of the attack rather than its definition, and both explanations produce exactly that consequence, which is why it cannot be decisive; the same is true of the third fact, since the treatment of data bears on ransomware or a data-integrity incident rather than on identifying a DoS attack. The capacity warning in the fourth fact supports the rival explanation. This question turns on separating the symptom, which is shared, from the mechanism, which is not.

questions.question:
Case: Employees of Hiranyakash Cashew Ltd received text messages sent in the name of a reputed grocery-delivery platform. In batch A the messages asked recipients to share their personal details to receive a free hamper. In batch B the messages asked recipients to install a "free tracking app", which then copied the contact list from the handsets. No voice call and no email accompanied either batch.
Which one of the following combinations applies the source's descriptions most correctly to the two batches?
options: Batch A - vishing; batch B - smishing.
Batch A - smishing; batch B - phishing through the SMS channel, the object being a download, together with mobile malware for the installed program.
Both batches - smishing, because both were text messages sent in the name of a reputable company, and the object of the message does not change the sub-type into which the message falls.
Batch A - whaling; batch B - domain spoofing.
questions.explanation: Smishing is described as sending text messages pretending from reputable companies to induce individuals to reveal personal information, and only batch A has that object, so batch A is the straightforward smishing case. The parent phishing description covers two objects, enticing a victim to share sensitive information such as passwords or to download a malicious file that will install viruses on their computer or phone, and the SMS channel is expressly listed, so batch B remains within phishing even though its object is installation of the app; that app, being malware designed to target mobile devices, also answers the mobile-malware subset. Treating both batches alike makes the channel the whole test, whereas two text messages with different objects fall in different categories, and in batch B the personal-information element is absent because the data was taken by the installed program rather than disclosed by the victim. Vishing requires calls or voice messages, whaling requires a senior-employee target and domain spoofing requires a fake website or domain, none of which is present.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct about the source's treatment of malware and its sub-types?
Statement 1: Malware is defined by reference to the intent with which a program or code is created, not by reference to whether harm was in fact caused.
Statement 2: A legitimate utility which came with the system and is then abused by an attacker to execute a cyber-attack falls outside the malware sub-types, because such a utility was not created with intent to do harm.
Statement 3: The four listed sub-types of malware are the only common types of cyber-attack recognised by the source.
Statement 4: Mobile malware is distinguished from the other sub-types by the platform it is designed to target.
options: Statements 1, 2 and 4 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1, 3 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Malware is any program or code created with intent to do harm to a computer, network or server, so the criterion is the purpose of creation and statement 1 is correct; statement 4 is equally correct, since mobile malware is defined simply as any type of malware designed to target mobile devices. Statement 2 is wrong in its conclusion, because the source expressly accommodates the case of an abused legitimate utility by describing fileless malware as malicious activity which uses legitimate tools built into the system to execute a cyber-attack, so the absence of a purpose-built malicious file does not place the activity outside the malware sub-types. Statement 3 is wrong because the four items are subsets of malware, while denial-of-service attacks, phishing and spoofing stand separately among the common types of cyber-attack; the combinations admitting either of those two statements therefore fail.

questions.category: Cyber Risks – Cyber Risks: classification exercise
questions.question:
Match each type of cyber-attack in Column I with the feature which the source treats as decisive for identifying it in Column II.
Column I: A. Malware  B. Denial-of-Service attack  C. Phishing  D. Spoofing
Column II: 1. A person is enticed, through email, SMS, phone or social media, either to give out sensitive information or to obtain a file which installs viruses.
2. A program or code was created with the intent to do harm to a computer, network or server.
3. A network is flooded with false requests so as to disrupt business operations, leaving users unable to perform routine tasks.
4. The attacker is disguised as a known or trusted source in order to reach targeted devices.
Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: Malware is defined by the intent behind the program or code, so A-2; a Denial-of-Service attack is defined by flooding a network with false requests to disrupt business operations, with the inability to perform routine tasks as its stated consequence, so B-3; phishing is defined by its four channels and its two objects of enticement, so C-1; and spoofing is defined by disguising the cybercriminal as a known or trusted source in order to access targeted devices, so D-4. The matching which exchanges phishing and spoofing is the one to watch, because an incident using a fake domain or a forged sender address can satisfy both descriptions, and the source itself links them by calling domain spoofing a form of phishing, yet the decisive feature of phishing remains the enticement of the person and that of spoofing the disguise of the sender. The matching which gives the enticement feature to malware and the intent-based definition to phishing fails because malware is defined simply by the intent with which a program or code is created, irrespective of the channel by which it is delivered, while phishing is defined by the channel and the enticement. The matching which gives the flood of false requests to spoofing and the disguise to the Denial-of-Service attack confuses the mechanism of disruption with the abuse of trust, and the source attaches the inability to perform routine tasks such as accessing email, websites or online accounts only to the former.

questions.category: Cyber Risks – Cyber-attack: meaning and intents
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A cybercriminal's attempt to gain unauthorized access to a network which succeeds only in exposing confidential data, the data being neither altered, disabled nor destroyed, still falls within the source's definition of a cyber-attack.
Reason (R): The source states the intents of a cyber-attack in the alternative, namely to damage, steal, expose, alter, disable or destroy data, so any one of them satisfies the definition.
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct, but R is incorrect.
A is incorrect, but R is correct.
questions.explanation: A cyber-attack is defined as an attempt to gain unauthorized access to a computing system or network with intent to damage, steal, expose, alter, disable or destroy data, and the six intents are joined by "or". Exposing data is one of the six, so the outcome described in the assertion brings the attempt within the definition and A is correct. R states precisely the disjunctive structure which produces that result, so it is not merely a true statement standing beside the assertion but the reason why exposure alone suffices. The second option is the plausible alternative for a candidate who reads the definition as requiring a cumulative effect; the third would follow only if "expose" were absent from the list, and the fourth only if the definition required all six intents.

questions.category: Cyber Risks – Cyber Risks: classification exercise
questions.question: Which one of the following represents the correct sequence from the MOST specific category to the BROADEST category, using only the source's own classification?
options: Whaling - Malware - Cyber-attack
Whaling - Phishing - Cyber-attack
Phishing - Whaling - Cyber-attack
Cyber-attack - Phishing - Whaling
questions.explanation: Whaling is given in the phishing table as a type of social-engineering attack within phishing, so it is a sub-type of phishing; phishing is in turn listed among the most common types of cyber-attack; and cyber-attack is the top-level concept of the whole discussion. That fixes the order as whaling, then phishing, then cyber-attack. Placing malware between whaling and cyber-attack reads malware as the parent of whaling, whereas the source's malware subsets are ransomware, fileless malware, Trojan and mobile malware, phishing and malware being siblings under cyber-attack rather than one inside the other. The remaining two options give the parent-to-child order and the broad-to-specific order, the latter being the reverse of what the question asks.

questions.category: Cyber Risks – Cyber Risks: classification exercise
questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct about the structure of the source's classification of cyber-attacks?
Statement 1: Ransomware, fileless malware, Trojan and mobile malware are presented as subsets of malware, and malware is in turn one of the common types of cyber-attack.
Statement 2: Spear phishing, whaling, smishing and vishing are presented as sub-types of phishing, and phishing is one of the common types of cyber-attack.
Statement 3: The source places domain spoofing among the types of spoofing while also calling it a form of phishing, so its categories are not mutually exclusive.
Statement 4: A denial-of-service attack is presented as a subset of malware, because flooding a network with false requests requires malicious code.
options: Statements 1 and 4 only
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 restate the nesting of the two tables, four subsets beneath malware and four sub-types beneath phishing, with malware, denial-of-service attacks, phishing and spoofing standing side by side as common types of cyber-attack. Statement 3 is the structurally important one, because the source's own wording describes domain spoofing as a form of phishing, so an attack may answer simultaneously to the spoofing and the phishing descriptions. Statement 4 is wrong, since denial-of-service is listed as a separate common type of cyber-attack rather than beneath malware, and the source attributes to it a flood of false requests rather than the running of malicious code, so no subset relationship exists; the three combinations which admit statement 4 therefore fail.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct about the distinctions drawn by the source?
options: Spear phishing is the phishing sub-type directed at specific individuals or organizations, typically through malicious emails.
Whaling is the phishing sub-type described as a social-engineering attack specifically targeting senior employees, with the purpose of stealing money or information.
Smishing and vishing are distinguished from one another by the channel used, text messages on the one hand and calls and voice messages on the other, both pretending from reputable companies.
Email spoofing and phishing differ in that email spoofing, unlike phishing, requires the attacker to encrypt data before asking for payment.
questions.explanation: The last statement is the incorrect one, because it attaches to email spoofing the two features the source reserves for ransomware, encryption of the victim's data and a decryption key offered in exchange for payment. Email spoofing is instead described as a cyberattack which targets businesses by using emails with forged sender addresses, and its family relationship is with the general spoofing concept of disguising the attacker as a known or trusted source. The first three statements are each supported: the spear-phishing description turns on targeting specific individuals or organizations typically through malicious emails, the whaling description turns on senior employees and on money or information, and smishing and vishing share the pretence of a reputable source while differing in the text-message against voice channel. Treating any payment-related incident as involving encryption is the misconception this question targets.

questions.question:
Meridian Textiles Ltd appointed its statutory auditor to review the design of its cyber-risk governance. The CFO described the company's practices as follows:
(i) Once each year the company performs a formal risk assessment and prepares a strategy addressing its principal cyber exposures.
(ii) It has deployed role-based access controls and encryption to safeguard its customer database.
(iii) It runs a round-the-clock monitoring desk intended to spot cybersecurity incidents as early as possible.
(iv) After a recent incident the board documented how it would communicate and act during a future event and prepared a forward action plan.
(v) Following that incident the company restored its ERP from backups and resumed normal operations within three days.
The incident itself had the following effects: the processing plant was shut for two days creating an operational problem; customers' personal information was leaked to the public; a regulator initiated legal proceedings against the company and imposed a monetary penalty; and the company paid substantial fees to external investigators to look into and remediate the matter.

Within the Cyber Security Framework described in the study material, which elements do practice (iv) and practice (v) respectively represent?
options: (iv) Detect; (v) Recover
(iv) Respond; (v) Recover
(iv) Respond; (v) Protect
(iv) Identify; (v) Recover
questions.explanation: The framework's Respond element requires the entity to have response planning and to assess future action plans, which is exactly what practice (iv) documents - a communication/acting plan and a forward action plan for a future event. The Recover element requires the entity to undertake appropriate actions to recover from an attack, which practice (v) performs by restoring the ERP from backups and resuming operations. Option A is wrong because (iv) is not about timely identification of risks (Detect). Option C is wrong because (v) restores after the event rather than implementing data-security controls (Protect). Option D mislabels (iv) as Identify, which concerns periodic risk assessment and strategy, not response planning.

questions.question:
Meridian Textiles Ltd appointed its statutory auditor to review the design of its cyber-risk governance. The CFO described the company's practices as follows:
(i) Once each year the company performs a formal risk assessment and prepares a strategy addressing its principal cyber exposures.
(ii) It has deployed role-based access controls and encryption to safeguard its customer database.
(iii) It runs a round-the-clock monitoring desk intended to spot cybersecurity incidents as early as possible.
(iv) After a recent incident the board documented how it would communicate and act during a future event and prepared a forward action plan.
(v) Following that incident the company restored its ERP from backups and resumed normal operations within three days.
The incident itself had the following effects: the processing plant was shut for two days creating an operational problem; customers' personal information was leaked to the public; a regulator initiated legal proceedings against the company and imposed a monetary penalty; and the company paid substantial fees to external investigators to look into and remediate the matter.

Consider the following statements mapping Meridian's practices to framework elements. 1. Practice (i) corresponds to the 'Identify' element. 2. Practice (ii) corresponds to the 'Protect' element. 3. Practice (iii) corresponds to the 'Detect' element. 4. Practice (i) corresponds to the 'Respond' element. Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: 'Identify' requires the entity to conduct periodic risk assessment and develop a strategy, so practice (i)'s annual assessment and strategy is a correct match. 'Protect' requires implementing effective controls for data security, so practice (ii)'s access controls and encryption correctly map to it. 'Detect' requires controls that identify cybersecurity risks timely, so practice (iii)'s monitoring desk correctly maps to it. Statement 4 is incorrect because the annual risk assessment and strategy is an Identify activity, not Respond, which concerns response planning for adverse events; this eliminates every option containing statement 4.

Stage 2 of the cyber-risk stages lists several possible consequences of a cyber event. All of the following consequences are actually illustrated by the incident described above, EXCEPT:
options: Business interruption causing an operational challenge
Breach of privacy
Intellectual property theft
Incident response cost for investigations and remediation
questions.explanation: Stage 2 lists seven consequences: business interruption, data loss/reputational loss/litigation, intellectual property theft, breach of privacy, incident response cost for investigations and remediation, regulatory costs, and fines and penalties. The described facts illustrate business interruption (plant shut for two days), breach of privacy (personal information leaked), litigation and penalties (regulator's proceedings and monetary penalty) and incident response cost (fees to external investigators). Intellectual property theft is on the Stage-2 list but no fact shows designs, patents or proprietary information being taken, so it is the consequence NOT illustrated. The other three options each have a direct supporting fact and therefore cannot be the exception.

Meridian Textiles Ltd appointed its statutory auditor to review the design of its cyber-risk governance. The CFO described the company's practices as follows:
(i) Once each year the company performs a formal risk assessment and prepares a strategy addressing its principal cyber exposures.

Assertion (A): Meridian's exposure is best characterised as a business risk affecting the whole organisation, not merely an IT problem. Reason (R): The consequences the study material enumerates for a cyber event - operational interruption, litigation, reputational harm, fines and investigation costs - fall on the business as a whole and are not confined to the IT function.
options: Both A and R are correct, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are correct, but R does not correctly explain A
A is correct, but R is incorrect
A is incorrect, but R is correct
questions.explanation: Stage 2 expressly states that cyber risks are not an issue of IT alone but a business risk affecting the whole business organisation, so Assertion A is correct. The same Stage-2 framing then substantiates that characterisation by listing consequences such as business interruption, litigation, reputational loss, fines and incident-response cost - harms borne across the enterprise rather than within the IT department. Because R identifies exactly those business-wide consequences as the basis for treating cyber risk as a business risk, R correctly explains A. Neither statement is incorrect, so options C and D fail; and the consequence list is genuinely the reason for the business-risk characterisation, so option B (correct but non-explanatory) also fails.

Meridian Textiles Ltd appointed its statutory auditor to review the design of its cyber-risk governance. The CFO described the company's practices as follows:
(i) Once each year the company performs a formal risk assessment and prepares a strategy addressing its principal cyber exposures.
(ii) It has deployed role-based access controls and encryption to safeguard its customer database.
(iii) It runs a round-the-clock monitoring desk intended to spot cybersecurity incidents as early as possible.
(iv) After a recent incident the board documented how it would communicate and act during a future event and prepared a forward action plan.
(v) Following that incident the company restored its ERP from backups and resumed normal operations within three days.
The incident itself had the following effects: the processing plant was shut for two days creating an operational problem; customers' personal information was leaked to the public; a regulator initiated legal proceedings against the company and imposed a monetary penalty; and the company paid substantial fees to external investigators to look into and remediate the matter.

Meridian's board now wishes to formally benchmark its existing security programme against applicable regulatory requirements. In the study material's 'Stages of Cyber Risks', this activity belongs primarily to:
options: The framework's Detect element (timely identification of risks)
Stage 2 - Impact of Cyber Risk
Stage 3 - Managing the Cyber Risk
The framework's Protect element (data-security controls)
questions.explanation: Stage 3 (Managing the Cyber Risk) states that a strategic approach helps an organisation assess its existing cybersecurity programme against regulatory requirements, which is precisely the benchmarking activity described. It is not Stage 2, which concerns the consequences/impact of a cyber event rather than programme evaluation. It is not the framework's Detect or Protect elements, which concern timely identification controls and data-security controls respectively, not a regulatory benchmark. The decisive fact is the phrase 'assess existing cybersecurity programme against regulatory requirements', a stated purpose of Stage 3.

questions.question:
Kaveri Payments Pvt Ltd processes vendor payments electronically. During an audit the following facts were established:
(1) A system administrator who had resigned six months earlier still held an active user ID that could edit the vendor master file.
(2) An outsider, using a password this person had reused from a breached shopping website, logged into the finance portal and altered a vendor's bank-account details, which were then used to divert a payment.
(3) Vendor master changes at Kaveri are requested by plain email to the finance team and are applied without any authentication step.
(4) The officer who releases wire transfers received a fraudulent email that impersonated a senior executive and demanded an urgent transfer; the officer had never received any awareness input about such scam techniques.
(5) Kaveri had no documented programme for installing vendor security fixes, and a known unpatched flaw in its server software was exploited.

Regarding fact (3) (vendor master changes requested by plain email and applied without authentication), which of the following control considerations from the study material are directly relevant? 1. Whether other communication channels (email) are used to request changes to master data. 2. Whether authentication protocols are defined to verify modifications to master data. 3. Whether the entity runs periodic vulnerability scans to identify unapplied patches. 4. Who is responsible for making changes to master data.
options: 1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The master-data control group asks who is responsible for master-data changes, whether other communication channels such as email are used to request them, what systems initiate/process such requests, and whether authentication protocols verify the modifications - so statements 1, 2 and 4 are all directly engaged by fact (3). Statement 3 is a patch-management consideration, which addresses unapplied software fixes and does not bear on the vendor-master change workflow, so it is not relevant here. Any option that includes statement 3 is therefore wrong, which eliminates the distractors that contain it.

questions.question:
Kaveri Payments Pvt Ltd processes vendor payments electronically. During an audit the following facts were established:
(1) A system administrator who had resigned six months earlier still held an active user ID that could edit the vendor master file.
(2) An outsider, using a password this person had reused from a breached shopping website, logged into the finance portal and altered a vendor's bank-account details, which were then used to divert a payment.
(3) Vendor master changes at Kaveri are requested by plain email to the finance team and are applied without any authentication step.
(4) The officer who releases wire transfers received a fraudulent email that impersonated a senior executive and demanded an urgent transfer; the officer had never received any awareness input about such scam techniques.
(5) Kaveri had no documented programme for installing vendor security fixes, and a known unpatched flaw in its server software was exploited.

Fact (1) - the resigned administrator retaining active vendor-master edit access - most directly exemplifies which concept in the study material?
options: Identity-based attack, because a user ID and password are involved
Insider threat, because a former employee retains direct access to the network and its data
DNS tunneling, because privileged data is moved across the network
IoT-based attack, because a server is targeted
questions.explanation: The study material defines insider threats as danger posed by current OR former employees because they have direct access to the company network, sensitive data or other information; a resigned administrator who still holds edit rights to the vendor master is exactly such a former employee with direct access. The decisive fact is that the person is a FORMER employee whose access persists, which the insider-threat concept expressly covers. Option A is wrong because the identity-based-attack idea (credential reuse across accounts) is what fact (2) illustrates, not the dormant account in fact (1). Options C and D describe unrelated attack techniques that have nothing to do with a lingering employee account.

questions.question:
Kaveri Payments Pvt Ltd processes vendor payments electronically. During an audit the following facts were established:
(1) A system administrator who had resigned six months earlier still held an active user ID that could edit the vendor master file.
(2) An outsider, using a password this person had reused from a breached shopping website, logged into the finance portal and altered a vendor's bank-account details, which were then used to divert a payment.

(5) Kaveri had no documented programme for installing vendor security fixes, and a known unpatched flaw in its server software was exploited.

Fact (4) - a wire-transfer officer who received a fraudulent urgent-transfer email and had never received awareness input on such scam techniques - is most directly addressed by which control consideration in the study material?
options: Controls around patch management
Controls around vendor setup and modifications (master data)
Controls around electronic transfer of funds - educating wire-transfer staff on phishing-scam threats
Controls around data backup and recovery
questions.explanation: The electronic-transfer-of-funds control group explicitly asks whether the persons responsible for wire transfers are educated on threats related to phishing scams, which directly matches the officer's lack of awareness input described in fact (4). This item is used here as a control consideration; it does not depend on the definition of the underlying scam technique. It is not a patch-management matter (which concerns software fixes, fact (5)) nor a master-data matter (facts (1)-(3)), and no control consideration in the table concerns backup and recovery. The decisive fact is that the person affected is the wire-transfer releaser, tying the control to the funds-transfer group.

questions.question:
Kaveri Payments Pvt Ltd processes vendor payments electronically. During an audit the following facts were established:
(1) A system administrator who had resigned six months earlier still held an active user ID that could edit the vendor master file.
(2) An outsider, using a password this person had reused from a breached shopping website, logged into the finance portal and altered a vendor's bank-account details, which were then used to divert a payment.
(3) Vendor master changes at Kaveri are requested by plain email to the finance team and are applied without any authentication step.

(5) Kaveri had no documented programme for installing vendor security fixes, and a known unpatched flaw in its server software was exploited.

Fact (2) - an outsider reusing a password leaked from a shopping website to log into the finance portal - is most accurately characterised under the study material as:
options: An insider threat, because the login used a legitimate user ID
DNS tunneling, because network access was obtained
A patch-management failure
An identity-based attack, because valid credentials were compromised and, since the same user ID/password served two accounts, possession of one account's credentials granted access to the other
questions.explanation: The material describes identity-based attacks as occurring when valid user credentials are compromised and the adversary pretends to be that user, illustrating that people often reuse the same user ID and password across accounts so that credentials for one account grant access to another. Fact (2) is a textbook instance: the attacker obtained valid credentials from the breached shopping site and used them to log into a second account, the finance portal. Option A fails because the attacker is an external outsider, not a current or former employee with direct access (which is what the insider-threat fact (1) captures). Options B and C invoke unrelated techniques - DNS-query abuse and software patching - that play no part in this credential-reuse compromise.

questions.question:
Kaveri Payments Pvt Ltd processes vendor payments electronically. During an audit the following facts were established:
(1) A system administrator who had resigned six months earlier still held an active user ID that could edit the vendor master file.
(2) An outsider, using a password this person had reused from a breached shopping website, logged into the finance portal and altered a vendor's bank-account details, which were then used to divert a payment.
(3) Vendor master changes at Kaveri are requested by plain email to the finance team and are applied without any authentication step.

(5) Kaveri had no documented programme for installing vendor security fixes, and a known unpatched flaw in its server software was exploited.

Fact (5) (no patch programme; a known unpatched flaw exploited) most directly engages which combination of control considerations? 1. Whether the entity has a patch management program. 2. Whether the entity runs periodic vulnerability scans to identify unapplied patches. 3. How the entity is notified of patches by external vendors. 4. Whether authentication protocols are defined to verify wire-transfer requests.
options: 1 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: The patch-management control group consists of exactly three questions: whether the entity has a patch management programme, whether it runs periodic vulnerability scans to identify unapplied patches, and how it is notified of patches by external vendors - so statements 1, 2 and 3 all bear on fact (5). The unpatched flaw being exploited maps to the absence of both a patch programme and vulnerability scanning. Statement 4 belongs to the electronic-transfer-of-funds group and concerns verifying wire-transfer requests, not software fixes, so it is irrelevant. Any option containing statement 4 is therefore wrong.

questions.question:
Nimbus IoT Logistics Ltd operates a fleet of connected delivery vehicles and smart sensors in its warehouses. Its statutory auditor noted the following during the year:
(A) An attacker used login credentials that a warehouse supervisor had reused across a personal social-media account and the company's driver portal, thereby signing in as the supervisor.
(B) Large volumes of shipment data were quietly moved out of the corporate network by embedding them inside ordinary domain-name-system (DNS) lookups, which the perimeter defences did not flag.
(C) A group of attackers disabled several warehouse temperature sensors by sending malicious commands directly to the connected devices.
(D) A current employee, without any harmful intent, emailed an internal file containing customer addresses to the wrong external recipient.
(E) The company had earlier considered the risk that an outsider could encrypt its dispatch software and demand payment, and the risk that fraudsters use email tricks to steal money.

Fact (B) is best classified under which cyber-attack type, and what is the decisive feature?
options: Identity-based attack - the attacker used a legitimate user's session
DNS tunneling - the data was transmitted by leveraging DNS queries to bypass traditional security measures
Denial-of-service - the sensors were overwhelmed by requests
Insider threat - an employee moved the shipment data out
questions.explanation: DNS tunneling is defined in the material as a cyberattack that leverages domain-name-system queries to bypass traditional security measures and transmit data within the network; fact (B) matches it exactly because the exfiltration was hidden inside ordinary DNS lookups that the perimeter did not flag. The decisive feature is that DNS queries are the transport that evades the defences. It is not an identity-based attack (no credential misuse is described in B), not a denial-of-service (nothing is flooded or disrupted), and not an insider threat (no employee access is involved). Options A, C and D each substitute an unrelated mechanism for the DNS-query abuse that defines the technique.

questions.question:
Nimbus IoT Logistics Ltd operates a fleet of connected delivery vehicles and smart sensors in its warehouses. Its statutory auditor noted the following during the year:
(A) An attacker used login credentials that a warehouse supervisor had reused across a personal social-media account and the company's driver portal, thereby signing in as the supervisor.
(B) Large volumes of shipment data were quietly moved out of the corporate network by embedding them inside ordinary domain-name-system (DNS) lookups, which the perimeter defences did not flag.
(C) A group of attackers disabled several warehouse temperature sensors by sending malicious commands directly to the connected devices.
(D) A current employee, without any harmful intent, emailed an internal file containing customer addresses to the wrong external recipient.
(E) The company had earlier considered the risk that an outsider could encrypt its dispatch software and demand payment, and the risk that fraudsters use email tricks to steal money.

Consider the following statements about facts (C) and (D). 1. Fact (C) is an IoT-based attack because the malicious commands targeted connected devices in the IoT network. 2. Fact (D) is an insider threat even though the employee acted without harmful intent, because insiders can pose danger through accidental activity. 3. Fact (D) cannot be an insider threat because insider threats always require malicious intent. 4. Fact (C) is DNS tunneling because data was moved out of the network. Which are correct?
options: 1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
questions.explanation: The material defines an IoT-based attack as any cyberattack that targets an Internet of Things device or network, so fact (C) - malicious commands sent directly to connected warehouse sensors - is correctly an IoT-based attack. It defines insider threats as danger from current or former employees with direct access, and the Stage-1 threat list expressly includes insiders committing malicious OR accidental activities, so fact (D) - a current employee carelessly emailing customer data - is an insider threat; statement 2 is therefore correct and statement 3 (requiring malicious intent) is wrong. Statement 4 is wrong because fact (C) does not use DNS queries to transport data, which is the defining feature of DNS tunneling (fact B). This leaves 1 and 2 correct.
