CA Surabhi is the group engagement partner.

WHAT CHANGES IF: during 2026 the Group decommissions the 2009 ERP and replaces it with the ledger vendor's own settlement module, so that no vendor-built interface between a legacy system and the ledger remains. The ledger continues to be shared with the Group's two external financiers. What is the effect on CA Surabhi's blockchain audit considerations under the source?
options: All of the blockchain audit implications fall away, because the source ties every one of them to the fact that blockchain interacts with legacy systems and business partners rather than to any independent concern.
The audit implications shift to the AI limb, since the vendor's replacement module will generate settlement data on a predictive basis using algorithms that cannot be seen directly.
Nothing changes at all, because the source's blockchain audit implications turn on the sequencing of blocks and the validation of each transaction rather than on any interface.

The insecure-API concern arising from the legacy interface falls away, but governance and security around transactions, the data confidentiality and privacy concerns arising because the ledger still interacts with business partners, and the compliance-liability determination all remain.
Only the compliance-liability limb remains, because data confidentiality and privacy are listed by the source among the challenges of NFTs and not among the considerations for blockchain.
questions.explanation: The source grounds the insecure-API concern in the fact that blockchain interacts with legacy systems and business partners, so removing the legacy interface removes that particular trigger while the business-partner trigger survives, because the ledger is still held by two external financiers. The fourth option therefore separates correctly what falls away from what survives. The first over-generalises by assuming every blockchain implication depends on legacy interaction, whereas governance and security around transactions and the compliance-liability determination stand independently. The second imports an AI consideration although the revised facts supply no predictive algorithm, and the third confuses the meaning paragraph, which explains sequencing and disqualification, with the audit-implications paragraph. The last misallocates confidentiality and privacy, which the source places in the blockchain audit implications as well as among NFT challenges. The decisive fact is the continued participation of external financiers in the ledger.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Where an audit client replaces stand-alone equipment with internet-connected devices and systems, the audit firm may have to train and upskill its auditors.
Reason (R): A shift to connected devices and systems may result in auditors not being able to rely only on manual controls, and the work that then has to be done is to evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of automated controls.

Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct, but R is incorrect.
Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is incorrect, but R is correct.
Both A and R are incorrect.
questions.explanation: The source's IoT audit implication runs in exactly this order: the shift to connected devices and systems may result in auditors not being able to rely only on manual controls, and audit firms may need to train and upskill auditors to evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of automated controls. R states the cause and the intervening task, and A states the resulting consequence, so R is the correct explanation of A rather than an unrelated true statement. The first alternative would apply if R recited something true but beside the point, such as the IoT key-risk list of device hijacking, data siphoning, denial of service attacks, data breaches and device theft. The second and fifth fail because R reproduces the source, and the fourth fails because A is expressly contemplated by it. The decisive point is that the loss of manual-only reliance is what creates the capability gap.

questions.category: Emerging Technologies – Risk attribution across technologies
questions.question: An engagement team records four observations about a client's new technology environment. Which observation is correctly matched to the technology whose listed key or common risks, under the source, the observed event belongs to?
options: A loan-scoring model declines applicants from certain localities far more often than the credit bureau data explains - matched to the key risks of Artificial Intelligence, because the source requires the review to look into how such patterns arise.

A client cannot open its own shipping records because the only person holding the required keys has resigned from the entity - matched to the key risks of the Internet of Things, since the records sit on devices the client no longer controls.

Unauthorised control of a client's connected cold-storage sensors, with readings secretly copied to an external address, together with a flood of false requests taking the monitoring desk offline - matched to the key risks of the Internet of Things.

Bots extended to four further processes before any operating or support model had been written - matched to the common risks of Blockchain, since the bots move value between systems without human intervention.
questions.explanation: The source's IoT key risks are device hijacking, data siphoning, denial of service attacks, data breaches and device theft, and the third observation describes the first, second and third of these in event form, so the attribution holds even though the observation is a compound one. The loan-scoring pattern is the strongest distractor: an unexplained locality effect is a matter the AI review must look into under the unintended-bias limb, but bias is not one of the three AI key risks, which the source limits to security, inappropriate configuration and data privacy. The resigned key-holder is dealt with by the source as a blockchain common risk, where inability to access data without required keys calls for specific protocols and contingency plans. Deploying bots without a support model is the RPA operational and execution risk, not a blockchain risk. The decisive step is distinguishing a named risk list from an audit implication.

questions.category: Emerging Technologies – Risk attribution across technologies
questions.question:
Column I lists technologies from the source's table of automated tools used as part of emerging technologies. Column II lists risk families in the words in which the source names them.

Column I
A. Internet of Things
B. Artificial Intelligence
C. Blockchain
D. Robotic Process Automation

Column II
1. Inability to reverse transactions and inability to access data without the required keys, so specific protocols and clear contingency plans are needed; exposure to cyber-attacks and data hacks because the system operates through network nodes.
2. Device hijacking, data siphoning, denial of service attacks, data breaches and device theft.
3. Operational and execution risk from deployment without a proper operating model; change management risk from not following the change management lifecycle; strategy risk from wrong expectations and unrealistic business goals.
4. Security, inappropriate configuration and data privacy.

Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: Each risk family in Column II is taken from one row of the source table, so the matching tests attribution rather than word association. Family 2 is the IoT key-risk list; family 4 is the AI key-risk list of security, inappropriate configuration and data privacy; family 1 is the blockchain common-risk paragraph built on the strength-that-is-also-a-weakness idea together with the network-node exposure; family 3 is the three named RPA risks. The pairing that swaps IoT and AI is the most common error because both rows speak of data. Placing the lock-out exposure with AI, or beginning from the wrong IoT list, or confusing blockchain with RPA, each breaks one of these links. The decisive point is that denial of service attacks appear in the source's IoT risk list only, so any option assigning family 2 away from A must fail.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): On a blockchain, the very features that make the system secure also oblige an organisation to lay down specific protocols and clear contingency plans.
Reason (R): Blockchain is a decentralised and distributed ledger secured through encryption, in which each transaction is validated by participants creating a block distributed to all participants, and all blocks are sequenced so that any modification or deletion of a block disqualifies the information.

Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct, but R is incorrect.
A is incorrect, but R is correct.
Both A and R are incorrect.
questions.explanation: Assertion A restates the source's blockchain common risk that strengths of blockchain can also be its weakness, and it identifies the operative features correctly: inability to reverse transactions and inability to access data without the required keys make the system secure but mean organisations need specific protocols to ensure they are not locked out and have clear contingency plans. Reason R is also a faithful statement of the source's blockchain meaning paragraph, but it explains only how integrity of the record is assured through validation, distribution and sequencing, and says nothing about irreversibility of a transaction or dependence on keys. Because the causal bridge the assertion needs is absent, R does not explain A even though both are true. The decisive distinction is that immutability of the recorded block and irreversibility of the transaction are different propositions in the source, so 'both correct and R explains A' is not available.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about the blockchain technology described in the source are correct?

Statement 1: The ledger is decentralised and distributed and is secured through encryption.
Statement 2: Each transaction is validated by blockchain participants, creating a block of information that is distributed to all participants.
Statement 3: All blocks are sequenced so that any modification or deletion of a block disqualifies the information.
Statement 4: Because each transaction is validated by participants, the platform guarantees that the data first entered was accurate.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 reproduce the three elements of the source's blockchain meaning: a decentralised and distributed ledger secured through encryption; each transaction validated by blockchain participants creating a block distributed to all participants; and all blocks sequenced so that any modification or deletion of a block disqualifies the information. Statement 4 is the inference the source does not permit, because validation and sequencing address whether a recorded block has been tampered with, not whether the entry was correct when first made - which is why a weight-entry error that cannot be reversed persists in the ledger indefinitely. The combinations admitting Statement 4 must fail, and the combination dropping Statement 1 omits the encryption and decentralised-ledger attributes that the source states first. The decisive distinction is between integrity against alteration and accuracy at origin.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about Artificial Intelligence, as treated in the source, is NOT correct?
options: AI refers to a system or a machine that can think and learn.
AI systems utilise data analysis and algorithms to make decisions based on predictive methods.
The key risks associated with AI are security, inappropriate configuration and data privacy.
The review of AI should ascertain whether unintended bias is added to algorithms, and auditors should assess the effectiveness of algorithms and whether output is reviewed.
Because algorithms are of an invisible nature, the auditor should replace any consideration of the logical flow of processes with a direct inspection of the algorithms themselves.
questions.explanation: The source's AI audit implication is that, due to the invisible nature of algorithms, audits must focus on the logical flow of processes; the last statement draws the opposite inference, treating invisibility as a reason to inspect the algorithms directly, which is exactly what the source says cannot be done. The first two statements reproduce the source's meaning paragraph, that AI is a system or machine that can think and learn and that AI systems use data analysis and algorithms to make decisions on a predictive basis. The third is the complete AI key-risk list, and the fourth combines the two remaining audit implications concerning unintended bias, algorithm effectiveness and review of output. The decisive test is what the auditor does with invisible algorithms, and the source answers it by redirecting attention to logical flow rather than to inspection of the model.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about Artificial Intelligence, as treated in the source, is/are NOT correct?

Statement 1: Since AI systems use algorithms that cannot be seen, the auditor's assessment of the effectiveness of algorithms can be dispensed with once the auditor is satisfied that output is reviewed by a person.
Statement 2: AI systems utilise data analysis and algorithms to make decisions based on predictive methods.
Statement 3: The source requires the AI review to ascertain whether intended business rules have been deliberately encoded as bias in the algorithms.
Statement 4: The key risks associated with AI are security, inappropriate configuration and data privacy.
options: 1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
3 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is not correct because the source lists two separate requirements - assessing effectiveness of algorithms and assessing whether output is reviewed - and a human review of output is not a substitute for the first. Statement 3 is not correct because the source requires the review to ascertain whether unintended bias is added to algorithms; a deliberately encoded business rule is a different proposition and is not what the auditor is asked to look for. Statements 2 and 4 are correct recitals of the source's meaning paragraph and its AI key-risk list respectively, so the combination treating them as incorrect is wrong, and the combination isolating only Statement 3 understates the errors. The decisive words are 'unintended' in the bias limb and the conjunction joining algorithm effectiveness to output review.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): An audit team that has no understanding of the tools used to develop and maintain a client's RPA bots has not met the RPA audit implication stated by the source, even if it fully understands the RPA data steps.
Reason (R): The source states that it is of utmost importance for auditors to understand RPA processes, which include data extraction, aggregation, sanitization and cleansing, and that this understanding alone places the auditor in a position to initiate and carry through the audit of an RPA-driven process.

Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct, but R is incorrect.
A is incorrect, but R is correct.
Both A and R are incorrect.
questions.explanation: Assertion A is correct because the source imposes a second, separate obligation on the auditor for RPA, namely that auditors must have an understanding of the tools used to develop and maintain RPA, which process knowledge alone does not satisfy. Reason R is incorrect as stated, because the source's process-understanding limb is expressed as the condition for being in a position to initiate the audit, and R converts it into a sufficient condition for the whole audit by adding the word 'alone' and by omitting the tools requirement. Since R misstates the source, neither of the two 'both correct' alternatives is available. The fourth and fifth fail because A is right. The decisive point is that the source sets out two distinct RPA requirements, and a reason that collapses them into one cannot be correct.

questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT an audit implication the source states for the technology against which it is placed?
options: IoT: a shift to connected devices and systems may result in auditors not being able to rely only on manual controls.
AI: audits must focus on the logical flow of processes because of the invisible nature of algorithms.
Blockchain: the auditor must assess the effectiveness of algorithms and whether output is reviewed.
RPA: it is of utmost importance to understand RPA processes, including data extraction, aggregation, sanitization and cleansing, otherwise the auditor will not be in a position to initiate the audit.
IoT: audit firms may need to train and upskill auditors to evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of automated controls.
questions.explanation: Assessing the effectiveness of algorithms and whether output is reviewed is the source's AI audit implication, not a blockchain one, so the third placement is the misattribution sought. The first and fifth options are the two limbs of the source's IoT audit implication, quoted substantially in the source's own words. The second is the AI implication driven by the invisibility of algorithms, and the fourth is the RPA precondition to initiating the audit. Every statement in this question is a genuine source sentence, so the decisive step is checking each against the technology row it is tagged to rather than against whether it is true somewhere in the table. Blockchain's audit implications are governance and security around transactions, insecure APIs and confidentiality where the ledger interacts with legacy systems and business partners, and determining whether blockchain data exposes the enterprise to liability for non-compliance with laws and regulations.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct?

Statement 1: NFT means something is unique and cannot be replaced, and NFTs are digital assets such as photos, videos, artwork and sports collectibles.
Statement 2: NFTs are tokens used to represent ownership of unique items, are secured by blockchain, and can only have one official owner at a time.
Statement 3: The source's key feature headed 'Unique' expresses itself in the proposition that an NFT cannot be forged.
Statement 4: NFT exchanges take place with cryptocurrencies on specialist sites.
Statement 5: Because NFTs are secured by blockchain, the source treats inability to reverse transactions as one of the challenges of NFTs.
options: 1, 2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only
1, 3, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 restate the source's NFT meaning paragraph, including the illustrative digital assets - photos, videos, artwork and sports collectibles - and the propositions that NFTs are secured by blockchain and can have only one official owner at a time. Statements 3 and 4 restate two of the three NFT key features, the third being that an NFT is a digital asset, and the source glosses 'Unique' by saying it cannot be forged. Statement 5 is wrong in its allocation: the challenges the source lists for NFTs are ownership and copyright concerns, security risks, a market that is not that wide, and online frauds, whereas inability to reverse transactions appears in the source as a blockchain common risk. The decisive point is that the NFT row borrows blockchain only to explain how ownership is secured, not to import blockchain's risk list.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of events in the blockchain process as described in the source's meaning paragraph?
options: A transaction is created and written to a block; the block is then sequenced; participants validate the transaction once it is visible to them; and the block is finally distributed to all participants.

A transaction is validated by blockchain participants; a block of information is created; the block is distributed to all participants; the blocks are sequenced so that any modification or deletion of a block disqualifies the information.

The blocks are sequenced on the distributed ledger; a transaction is then validated by participants; the resulting block is distributed to all participants; and any modification of a block then creates a new block.
A block is distributed to all participants; participants then validate the transaction; the ledger is encrypted; and the blocks are sequenced so that modification disqualifies the information.
questions.explanation: The source's blockchain meaning paragraph sets out validation of each transaction by blockchain participants, the creation of a block of information as a result, distribution of that block to all participants, and sequencing of all blocks so that any modification or deletion of a block disqualifies the information. The second option follows that order and preserves the stated consequence of sequencing. The first writes the block and sequences it before validation, reversing the causal order the source uses. The third begins with sequencing, which is the last step, and substitutes creation of a new block for disqualification of the information. The fourth places distribution before validation and turns encryption, which the source states as a general attribute of the ledger, into a step. The decisive point is that distribution and sequencing are consequences of validation, not conditions for it.

questions.category: Emerging Technologies – Integrated (IoT, AI, Blockchain, RPA, NFT)
questions.question: CA Surabhi is drafting the technology-assurance section of her group audit plan for an entity that has adopted IoT, Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, NFTs and RPA together. Which one of the following statements in her draft is NOT correct on the basis of the source?
options: Because AI algorithms are of an invisible nature, the audit of the AI-enabled underwriting process will focus on the logical flow of processes, and the review will ascertain whether unintended bias is added to the algorithms.

Before initiating the audit of the RPA-enabled invoice process, the team will understand the RPA processes, including data extraction, aggregation, sanitization and cleansing, and will also understand the tools used to develop and maintain the RPA.

The team's existing strength in manual controls means that the migration of the warehousing segment to connected devices does not by itself call for new capability, because manual review of system-generated summaries can be extended to cover connected devices.

Where the blockchain interacts with legacy systems and business partners, concerns related to insecure APIs, data confidentiality and privacy cannot be ignored, and the team must be able to determine whether data put on the blockchain will expose the enterprise to liability for non-compliance with laws and regulations.

Adoption of these technologies is being undertaken to create synergies and to harness the latest technologies, and the automated tools concerned include NFTs, which are secured by blockchain and can have only one official owner at a time.
questions.explanation: The third statement is the one that is not correct, because the source's IoT audit implication is that a shift to connected devices and systems may result in auditors not being able to rely only on manual controls and that audit firms may need to train and upskill auditors to evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of automated controls; manual review of system-generated summaries is precisely the kind of reliance the source says may be unavailable. The first statement restates the AI logical-flow and unintended-bias implications, and the second restates both limbs of the RPA implication. The fourth reproduces the blockchain audit implication, and the fifth reflects the introductory premise of the table together with the NFT row. The decisive fact is that the change is to connected devices, which is the trigger the source uses to displace manual-only reliance regardless of the team's existing manual-control strength.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about Robotic Process Automation, as treated in the source, are NOT correct?

Statement 1: RPA is the automation of repetitive processes performed by users and is a software technology that emulates human actions interacting with digital systems.
Statement 2: RPA software bots can interact with any application the same way people do, except that they can operate nonstop, much faster and with 100% reliability and precision.
Statement 3: The source attributes the 100% reliability and precision of RPA bots to the entity's general IT controls operating over the bot platform.
Statement 4: An auditor who understands the entity's general IT controls but not the RPA data steps is nevertheless in a position to initiate the audit.
options: 3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct recitals of the source's RPA meaning paragraph, so any combination listing them as not correct must fail. Statement 3 is not correct because the source states the nonstop operation, speed, reliability and precision as attributes of the software bots themselves in the meaning paragraph; it offers no origin for them and in particular does not derive them from general IT controls. Statement 4 is not correct because the source conditions the ability to initiate the audit on understanding the RPA processes, which include data extraction, aggregation, sanitization and cleansing, and says that otherwise the auditor will not be in a position to initiate the audit. The decisive point is that neither statement may be rescued by importing material from elsewhere in the chapter, since the question tests only what the RPA row says.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct?

Statement 1: IoT is the concept of connecting any device to the internet, the source illustrating the breadth of that description with cell phones, coffee makers and washing machines.
Statement 2: The key components of IoT are data collection, analytics, connectivity, people and process.
Statement 3: The source confines the effect of IoT to the entity's business model, leaving its strategic objectives to be settled by the board independently of the technology.
Statement 4: The response the source contemplates for audit firms is to train and upskill auditors to evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of automated controls.
options: 1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 reproduces the source's IoT meaning paragraph including its illustrative devices, which are given to show that the concept reaches any device and not merely industrial equipment. Statement 2 is the source's list of key components, and Statement 4 is the second limb of its audit implication, the first being that auditors may not be able to rely only on manual controls. Statement 3 is the failure: the source says in terms that IoT not only changes the business model but also affects strategic objectives of the organisation, so the effect cannot be confined to the business model with strategy left untouched. The combinations carrying Statement 3 therefore all fail, and the combination limited to Statements 1 and 2 wrongly drops the upskilling implication. The decisive words are 'not only... but also'.

questions.question:
Statement 1: A remote audit must be completely virtual; an audit that combines on-site procedures with online procedures is outside the meaning of a remote audit.
Statement 2: A remote audit or virtual audit is one in which the auditor uses online or electronic means to conduct the audit, and it could be partially or completely virtual.
Statement 3: Where the audit is conducted fully through electronic means, the source framework dispenses with the requirement of a documented risk assessment.
Statement 4: The considerations listed for a remote audit are feasibility and planning, confidentiality/security and data protection, and risk assessment.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 2 reproduces the source meaning correctly: a remote (virtual) audit uses online or electronic means and may be partially or completely virtual. Statement 4 matches the three consideration heads in the source table. Statement 1 is wrong because it applies the rule too narrowly - partial virtuality is expressly contemplated, so a hybrid still falls within the concept. Statement 3 is wrong because the risk assessment consideration requires that assessment be done and documented for each audit; the mode or degree of virtuality of the engagement does not remove that requirement.

questions.question:
Column I (Remote audit step) against Column II (Consideration under which the source table deals with it).
Column I:
A. Agreeing audit timelines and fixing Zoom or Google Meet as the meeting platform
B. Removing information reviewed and documented by the auditor from the document sharing platform
C. Performing and documenting the assessment for each audit
D. Using VPN while accessing the auditee's IT system
Column II:
1. Feasibility and Planning
2. Confidentiality, Security and Data Protection
3. Risk Assessment
Which of the following represents the correct matching?
questions.explanation: Timelines and the choice of meeting platform are expressly the content of the Feasibility and Planning row, so A-1. Removal of information reviewed and documented by the auditor, and the use of VPN when accessing the auditee's IT system, both sit in the Confidentiality, Security and Data Protection row, so B-2 and D-2. The requirement that assessment be done and documented for each audit is the whole content of the Risk Assessment row, so C-3. The attractive error is pairing C with confidentiality because documentation of working papers feels like a security matter, but the source places the 'done and documented for each audit' obligation squarely under risk assessment.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): An auditor conducting a remote audit may take screenshots of the auditee and retain them as audit evidence when the auditee is unable to furnish the underlying documents electronically.
Reason (R): Under the remote audit framework, information reviewed and documented by the auditor is to be removed from the document sharing platform.
In the context of the source material, which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct, but R is incorrect
A is incorrect, but R is correct
Both A and R are incorrect
questions.explanation: The source is categorical that the auditor should not take screenshots of auditees as audit evidence, and it admits no exception for uncooperative or unable auditees, so the Assertion fails. The Reason is a verbatim application of the confidentiality, security and data protection row, which requires information reviewed and documented by the auditor to be removed from the platform, so it is correct. The error in A is a classic conditional exception invented on top of an unconditional prohibition: inability to obtain documents electronically changes the auditor's evidence problem but not the screenshot rule.

questions.question:
CASE: Vikram & Associates is auditing Nexa Retail Ltd, whose branches and warehouses are spread over five states. Because of travel restrictions, the engagement partner decides that the audit will be conducted completely virtually. During planning, the team agrees audit timelines with the company, fixes Zoom as the meeting platform, and identifies one document-sharing platform to be used by the firm and the company. In due course: (i) the company's finance manager uploads scanned warehouse records to the sharing platform, the auditor reviews them, documents the procedures performed on them, and the copy is left on the platform until the audit report is signed; (ii) during a video meeting, the CFO asks the auditor to send a screenshot of the auditee's participation as "proof of attendance", and the auditor declines; (iii) the auditor accesses the company's ERP remotely using VPN rather than a direct internet connection; (iv) the firm performs and documents a separate risk assessment for this engagement, as it does for each of the five other group companies it audits remotely.
Which of the above statements about the case are correct?
Statement 1: In (i), retention of the reviewed records on the platform until the report is signed is permissible, because the removal requirement applies only to files the auditor personally uploaded and not to files uploaded by the company.
Statement 2: In (ii), declining to send a screenshot of the auditee as audit evidence accords with the source guidance on confidentiality, security and data protection.
Statement 3: In (iii), VPN is the means prescribed by the source for the auditor's access to the auditee's IT system.
Statement 4: In (iv), one common risk assessment documented once for the entire group would satisfy the source requirement, provided the companies' processes are similar.
options: 1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: the source expressly bars screenshots of auditees as audit evidence and expressly directs use of VPN where the auditor accesses the auditee's IT system, so both facts show compliant conduct. Statement 1 is wrong because the removal requirement is triggered by information reviewed and documented by the auditor, irrespective of who uploaded the file, so Nexa's retention of the reviewed warehouse records until signing breaches it. Statement 4 inverts the rule: assessment should be done and documented for each audit, and process similarity does not license a single group-level document; the decisive fact in (iv) is that the firm assessed each audit separately, which is the compliant pattern.

questions.question:
Statement 1: Access to the document sharing platform used for a remote audit should be restricted, and the data should be secured by encryption.
Statement 2: Information reviewed and documented by the auditor should be removed from the document sharing platform.
Statement 3: Once the platform is encrypted, reviewed information may remain on it for the life of the engagement, since retention on a secured platform carries no data-protection concern.
Statement 4: The taking of legislation and regulations into consideration is part of the feasibility and planning consideration for a remote audit.
Which of the above statements are correct as per the source?
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
All of the above
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 restate the confidentiality, security and data protection row, which requires restricted and encrypted access to the sharing platform and removal of information reviewed and documented by the auditor. Statement 3 applies the encryption safeguard too broadly: encryption addresses how data is protected while on the platform, but it does not displace the separate instruction that reviewed and documented information be removed. Statement 4 misclassifies the source: legislation and regulations are to be taken into consideration under the confidentiality, security and data protection head, not feasibility and planning, which covers timelines, meeting platform and the sharing platform.

questions.question: CASE: A partner objects to treating a mixed engagement as a remote audit: "Physical verification of the main plant's inventory will still be attended in person; only the remaining procedures are performed through online and electronic means, so the remote audit considerations cannot apply to the online portion." What changes if an audit is partially, rather than completely, virtual?
options: The remote audit considerations apply only where the audit is completely virtual, so they lapse for the hybrid portion
The engagement ceases to be a remote audit and is treated as a conventional audit that merely uses communication technology
Nothing changes as to applicability, because the remote audit could be partially or completely virtual, and the considerations are not graded by the extent of virtuality
Only the feasibility and planning consideration survives, because confidentiality and risk assessment presuppose a fully virtual audit
questions.explanation: The source defines a remote or virtual audit by the use of online or electronic means to conduct the audit and states that it could be partially or completely virtual. Partial physical verification therefore does not remove the engagement from the concept, and the three consideration heads continue to apply to the electronic part of the work, so the partner's objection applies the definition too narrowly. Options 1 and 4 create a threshold of virtuality that the source does not contain. Option 2 recharacterizes the engagement instead of applying the express partial-virtuality language, which is the decisive wording in the source.

questions.question: In planning a remote audit, the engagement team records the following steps. Which step is LEAST appropriately placed under the source's 'Feasibility and Planning' consideration?
options: Agreeing the audit timelines with the auditee before any audit session is conducted
Fixing Zoom or Google Meet as the platform on which the audit sessions will be held
Identifying, at the planning stage, the document sharing platform to be used by the firm and the auditee
Deciding that information reviewed and documented by the auditor will be removed from the platform after use
questions.explanation: Feasibility and planning in the source comprises agreeing audit timelines, the meeting platform (Zoom calls/Google Meet) and the document sharing platform, so options 1, 2 and 3 are correctly placed there. The removal of information reviewed and documented by the auditor is a data-protection rule from the confidentiality, security and data protection row, not a planning logistic. The trap is that deciding removal in advance 'feels' like planning; the decisive fact is that the subject matter of step 4 - handling of reviewed information on the platform - is governed by the consideration dealing with confidentiality, security and data protection.

questions.question:
CASE: Sage & Co., chartered accountants, are conducting remote audits for two clients - a tea processing company at Guwahati and an ocean-freight logistics company at Kochi whose vessels are currently at sea. The following facts emerge during the engagements: (P) the audit team works from a home environment and saves travel time and travel costs; (Q) evidence gathering for the tea company is spread over three weeks instead of a compressed ten-day field visit; (R) a network outage interrupts the video exit meeting with the Kochi team; (S) the Guwahati store-keeper emails scanned invoices whose printed dates do not agree with the entries discussed, and the team cannot rule out that documents were altered while relevant papers were withheld; (T) the team is unable to visualise the facility culture of the plant or the body language of supervisors during video interviews; (U) the Kochi company's IT head declines to permit remote access to the payroll and inventory servers, which are designated as sensitive; (V) the firm inducts a port-logistics specialist from its overseas member firm into the Kochi team; (W) physical verification of the fuel on the vessels and attendance at stock taking at the Guwahati warehouse cannot be carried out.
Which of the above statements about the classification of these facts under the source's advantages and disadvantages of remote audit are correct?
Statement 1: (P), (Q) and (V) each correspond to an advantage listed by the source.
Statement 2: (U) corresponds to the advantage that the auditor can get first-hand evidence directly from the IT system.
Statement 3: (R) and (T) both correspond to disadvantages listed by the source.
Statement 4: (S) illustrates the listed disadvantage that the opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information is increased.
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
All of the above
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct: (P) is cost and time effectiveness with no travel time or costs, (Q) is the spreading of evidence gathering over several weeks, and (V) is the widening of auditor selection from a global network of experts, while (R) is network interruption of interviews and meetings and (T) is the inability to visualise facility culture and body language, and (S) is the increased opportunity to present doctored documents and omit relevant information. Statement 2 is the deliberate confusion trap: the advantage of first-hand evidence directly from the IT system presupposes access being given, whereas (U) is the disadvantage that remote access to sensitive IT systems may not be allowed. The decisive fact in (U) is that the servers are designated sensitive and access was declined, so it belongs to the disadvantage column.

CASE: Sage & Co., chartered accountants, are conducting remote audits for two clients - a tea processing company at Guwahati and an ocean-freight logistics company at Kochi whose vessels are currently at sea. The following facts emerge during the engagements: (P) the audit team works from a home environment and saves travel time and travel costs; (Q) evidence gathering for the tea company is spread over three weeks instead of a compressed ten-day field visit; (R) a network outage interrupts the video exit meeting with the Kochi team; (S) the Guwahati store-keeper emails scanned invoices whose printed dates do not agree with the entries discussed, and the team cannot rule out that documents were altered while relevant papers were withheld; (T) the team is unable to visualise the facility culture of the plant or the body language of supervisors during video interviews; (U) the Kochi company's IT head declines to permit remote access to the payroll and inventory servers, which are designated as sensitive; (V) the firm inducts a port-logistics specialist from its overseas member firm into the Kochi team; (W) physical verification of the fuel on the vessels and attendance at stock taking at the Guwahati warehouse cannot be carried out.
Each of the following pairs one fact from the case with a source-listed effect. Which pairing is NOT correct?
options: (P) - Cost and time effective: no travel time and travel costs involved
(U) - Remote access to sensitive IT systems may not be allowed
(Q) - Opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information is increased
(W) - Audit procedures like physical verification of assets and stock taking cannot be performed
questions.explanation: (Q) is drawn from the advantage column: the time required to gather evidence can be spread over several weeks instead of a small period. The doctored-document point is a separate listed disadvantage which the case illustrates through (S), where altered dates and withheld papers are in issue, so pairing it with (Q) mixes two different rows. (P), (U) and (W) are each matched with the effect the source itself states: no travel time or costs as an advantage, sensitive-system remote access not allowed as a disadvantage, and physical verification of assets and stock taking not performable as a disadvantage.

questions.question:
CASE: Sage & Co., chartered accountants, are conducting remote audits for two clients - a tea processing company at Guwahati and an ocean-freight logistics company at Kochi whose vessels are currently at sea. The following facts emerge during the engagements: (P) the audit team works from a home environment and saves travel time and travel costs; (Q) evidence gathering for the tea company is spread over three weeks instead of a compressed ten-day field visit; (R) a network outage interrupts the video exit meeting with the Kochi team; (S) the Guwahati store-keeper emails scanned invoices whose printed dates do not agree with the entries discussed, and the team cannot rule out that documents were altered while relevant papers were withheld; (T) the team is unable to visualise the facility culture of the plant or the body language of supervisors during video interviews; (U) the Kochi company's IT head declines to permit remote access to the payroll and inventory servers, which are designated as sensitive; (V) the firm inducts a port-logistics specialist from its overseas member firm into the Kochi team; (W) physical verification of the fuel on the vessels and attendance at stock taking at the Guwahati warehouse cannot be carried out.
In response to facts (R) and (U), which of the following actions are consistent with the source's remote audit guidance?
Action 1: To reduce interruptions, shift exchange of audit records to an open unencrypted sharing application that does not depend on the meeting connection.
Action 2: For IT systems which the company does permit the auditor to access remotely, use VPN for such access.
Action 3: Perform and document a risk assessment for each of the two remote engagements before proceeding.
Action 4: Recognise (W) as one of the listed disadvantages of remote audit and address its implications for the related audit procedures during planning.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Action 1 is impermissible because access to the document sharing platform should be restricted and secured by encrypting data; an open unencrypted application breaches both limbs of that rule whatever the bandwidth motive. Action 2 applies the source's express direction that VPN be used where the auditor accesses the auditee's IT system, and Action 3 applies the requirement that assessment be done and documented for each audit, which remains binding even though two engagements share a platform. Action 4 correctly treats physical verification of assets and stock taking being non-performable as a listed disadvantage of remote audit to be recognised and planned around, which is the point the vessels-at-sea and warehouse facts raise.

questions.question:
CASE: Vikram & Associates is auditing Nexa Retail Ltd, whose branches and warehouses are spread over five states. Because of travel restrictions, the engagement partner decides that the audit will be conducted completely virtually. During planning, the team agrees audit timelines with the company, fixes Zoom as the meeting platform, and identifies one document-sharing platform to be used by the firm and the company. In due course: (i) the company's finance manager uploads scanned warehouse records to the sharing platform, the auditor reviews them, documents the procedures performed on them, and the copy is left on the platform until the audit report is signed; (ii) during a video meeting, the CFO asks the auditor to send a screenshot of the auditee's participation as "proof of attendance", and the auditor declines; (iii) the auditor accesses the company's ERP remotely using VPN rather than a direct internet connection; (iv) the firm performs and documents a separate risk assessment for this engagement, as it does for each of the five other group companies it audits remotely.
Assume that during a video walkthrough of a warehouse, the store official displays the stock register on his screen and invites the auditor to photograph it "for the audit file". Which of the following actions would be consistent with the source's remote audit framework?
Action 1: Decline to take the screen image, since the auditor should not take screenshots of auditees as audit evidence.
Action 2: Ask the company to place the register on the restricted, encrypted sharing platform instead, and remove the reviewed and documented information from it after use.
Action 3: Photograph the register but retain the image only on the auditor's own encrypted laptop, since the prohibition relates to the auditee's platform.
Action 4: Photograph the register only if the CFO grants written permission, since the prohibition is waivable.
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Action 1 applies the unqualified rule that the auditor should not take screenshots of auditees as audit evidence, so the invitation cannot be accepted in any form. Action 2 uses the compliant evidence channel: restricted and encrypted platform access, coupled with removal of information reviewed and documented by the auditor. Actions 3 and 4 misread the destination of the rule - it bars the auditor from taking such screenshots as audit evidence, so storing them on the auditor's own encrypted laptop does not cure the breach, and no consent or written waiver is contemplated by the source. The decisive fact is that the prohibition is on the act of capturing auditee screenshots as evidence, not on where the file is kept.

questions.question:
CASE: Vikram & Associates is auditing Nexa Retail Ltd, whose branches and warehouses are spread over five states. Because of travel restrictions, the engagement partner decides that the audit will be conducted completely virtually. During planning, the team agrees audit timelines with the company, fixes Zoom as the meeting platform, and identifies one document-sharing platform to be used by the firm and the company. In due course: (i) the company's finance manager uploads scanned warehouse records to the sharing platform, the auditor reviews them, documents the procedures performed on them, and the copy is left on the platform until the audit report is signed; (ii) during a video meeting, the CFO asks the auditor to send a screenshot of the auditee's participation as "proof of attendance", and the auditor declines; (iii) the auditor accesses the company's ERP remotely using VPN rather than a direct internet connection; (iv) the firm performs and documents a separate risk assessment for this engagement, as it does for each of the five other group companies it audits remotely.
In fact (i), the platform is encrypted throughout. What changes if the auditor defends leaving the reviewed and documented records on the platform until the report is signed on the ground that the data is encrypted?
options: Nothing changes - information reviewed and documented by the auditor is to be removed from the platform, and encryption of the data does not extend the permissible period of retention
The position changes, because the removal obligation operates only while meetings are being scheduled and not after the fieldwork is complete
The position changes, because the removal obligation attaches to auditor uploads, and here the finance manager uploaded the records
The obligation reverses - reviewed information must be preserved on the platform until the report is signed so that a trail remains available
questions.explanation: Encryption governs how the platform is secured while data is on it, whereas removal governs how long reviewed and documented information may stay there; the two instructions operate independently, so encryption adds nothing to the defence. Option 2 invents a timing limit and option 4 inverts the direction of the rule, neither of which finds support in the source. Option 3 is the fact-level distractor - the upload source is irrelevant because the trigger is the auditor's review and documentation, which is present on the case facts. The decisive fact is that the auditor both reviewed and documented these records, so removal was required regardless of the encryption status.

questions.question:
CASE: Vikram & Associates is auditing Nexa Retail Ltd, whose branches and warehouses are spread over five states. Because of travel restrictions, the engagement partner decides that the audit will be conducted completely virtually. During planning, the team agrees audit timelines with the company, fixes Zoom as the meeting platform, and identifies one document-sharing platform to be used by the firm and the company. In due course: (i) the company's finance manager uploads scanned warehouse records to the sharing platform, the auditor reviews them, documents the procedures performed on them, and the copy is left on the platform until the audit report is signed; (ii) during a video meeting, the CFO asks the auditor to send a screenshot of the auditee's participation as "proof of attendance", and the auditor declines; (iii) the auditor accesses the company's ERP remotely using VPN rather than a direct internet connection; (iv) the firm performs and documents a separate risk assessment for this engagement, as it does for each of the five other group companies it audits remotely.
Which of the above statements are correct?
Statement 1: The planning steps described - timelines, meeting platform and document sharing platform - fall under the source's feasibility and planning consideration.
Statement 2: The VPN usage in fact (iii) is unnecessary under the source, because the VPN direction applies to the document sharing platform and not to access to the auditee's IT systems.
Statement 3: The auditor's conduct in fact (ii) is correct, because screenshots of auditees should not be taken as audit evidence.
Statement 4: Because the engagement is completely virtual, fact (iv) shows a step that the source does not require.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 correctly identifies timelines and the selection of meeting and document sharing platforms as the content of the feasibility and planning consideration, and statement 3 correctly applies the prohibition on taking screenshots of auditees as audit evidence. Statement 2 reverses the source: the VPN direction is precisely for the case of accessing the auditee's IT system, as the ERP facts illustrate. Statement 4 is wrong because assessment should be done and documented for each audit, so the per-engagement risk assessment in (iv) is mandatory whatever the degree of virtuality; treating a completely virtual audit as an exception applies the concept too broadly.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): As per the source, the auditor getting first-hand evidence directly from the IT system is treated as an advantage of remote audit, while the fact that remote access to sensitive IT systems may not be allowed is treated as a disadvantage.
Reason (R): These two propositions contradict each other, so an auditee must elect which of them will apply to its audit.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct, but R is incorrect
A is incorrect, but R is correct
Both A and R are incorrect
questions.explanation: The Assertion is exactly the source treatment: the two propositions are listed in opposite columns of the same table, one under advantages and the other under disadvantages. The Reason is wrong because the source does not treat them as mutually exclusive and gives the auditee no election: the advantage describes the potential to draw evidence directly from the IT system where access is given, while the disadvantage describes the case where an entity designates systems as sensitive and does not allow remote access. The decisive distinction is between the general possibility and the permission outcome in a given engagement, which is why the option claiming both statements correct fails.

questions.question: The source lists among the advantages of a remote audit that the time required to gather evidence can spread over several weeks instead of a small period. Which of the following readings of this advantage is MOST faithful to the source?
options: Evidence gathering necessarily becomes shorter in total duration, which is why audit cost and time effectiveness arise
A longer gathering window automatically increases the risk of doctored documents, so this advantage is neutralised by a corresponding disadvantage
The spreading of evidence gathering is permissible only where physical verification of assets has already been completed
The advantage lies in the stretched window itself, which substitutes a several-week period for a compressed fieldwork spell, independent of the cost saving from no travel
questions.explanation: The source presents the spreading of evidence-gathering time over several weeks as a distinct advantage with its own rationale, separate from cost and time effectiveness arising from the absence of travel time and travel costs, which is how option 1 erroneously fuses two rows of the table. Option 2 borrows the doctored-document disadvantage and grafts a causal link onto this advantage that the source does not state. Option 3 imports a condition from the physical-verification disadvantage, but the source attaches no such precondition to the spread of evidence gathering. Option 4 correctly identifies the decisive point: the several-week window itself is the advantage.

questions.question: CASE: CA Nikhil's firm audits six unconnected small companies, each engagement being conducted through online and electronic means. He prepares a single remote audit risk assessment document covering all six companies, records the common observations once, and does not prepare or document an assessment for each engagement separately, arguing that similarity of processes makes this sufficient. Which option most accurately identifies the defect in this approach under the source?
options: No defect, because the requirement is satisfied once an assessment is performed and documented somewhere in the firm
The defect is that documentation should have been prepared before the meeting platform was finalised, since risk assessment belongs to feasibility and planning
The assessment should be done and documented for each audit, so a single common document defeats the per-audit requirement
The requirement is triggered only where the auditor accesses the auditee's IT system through VPN
questions.explanation: The source's risk assessment row states in full that assessment should be done and documented for each audit, which makes the unit of compliance the individual audit rather than the firm or the process profile. Six engagements therefore call for six documented assessments, and similarity of processes does not merge them. Option 1 reads the rule as a firm-level formality and option 4 wrongly conditions it on VPN-based IT system access, which belongs to a different consideration. Option 2 misclassifies the concept: risk assessment is its own consideration head, not a sub-set of feasibility and planning.

questions.question:
Statement 1: Where the document sharing platform encrypts all stored data, access controls to the platform may be left open to all auditee staff without violating the source's confidentiality guidance.
Statement 2: Screenshots of auditees may be taken as audit evidence if the auditee consents in writing.
Statement 3: Where the auditor accesses the auditee's IT system, the auditor should use VPN.
Statement 4: The auditor need not take legislation and regulations into consideration while planning the remote audit.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct as per the source?
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
All of the above
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are all incorrect. Access should be both restricted and secured by encryption, so encryption is not a substitute for restriction. The prohibition on screenshots of auditees as audit evidence contains no consent exception. The auditor should take legislation and regulations into consideration, which statement 4 denies. Statement 3 is the only correct one, as VPN is the source-prescribed means where the auditor accesses the auditee's IT system, so the option sets that include statement 3 among the incorrect ones must be rejected.

questions.question: Which pairing of a remote audit situation with its treatment in the source is correct?
options: A video interview is interrupted for twenty minutes by a network outage - efficiency is affected by time zone issues
Scanned vouchers are suspected to have altered dates - the auditor is unable to visualise the facility culture
A designated-sensitive payroll server is not opened to remote access - the auditor obtains first-hand evidence directly from the IT system
The company declines remote access to its servers on the ground that they are sensitive - remote access to sensitive IT systems may not be allowed
questions.explanation: Option 4 states the pairing exactly as the source does, since the non-permission of remote access to sensitive IT systems is a listed disadvantage and sensitivity of the servers is the decisive fact. Option 1 substitutes time zone issues for the listed disadvantage of network issues interrupting interviews and meetings; time zones are mentioned in a different row alongside the inability to visualise facility culture. Option 2 mixes the doctored-document disadvantage with the facility culture and body language one. Option 3 flips the sibling entry: inability to access is the disadvantage, while first-hand evidence from the IT system is the advantage available only when access exists.

questions.question:
CASE: For the financial year 2025-26, CA Divya accepts the remote audit of a manufacturer based at Chandigarh, with a plant at Uttarakhand and an export warehouse at Gujarat. She: (1) agrees the audit timelines with the company and fixes Google Meet as the meeting platform, with a document sharing platform also identified; (2) ensures that access to that platform is restricted and the data encrypted, and that the information she reviews and documents is removed from the platform; (3) schedules sessions at hours convenient to India, which requires an expert seconded from the firm's overseas member network to join very late at night, with discussions stretching and efficiency affected; (4) reuses for this engagement the risk assessment she had performed and documented for last year's remote audit of a different company with similar processes; (5) seeks VPN-based remote access to the plant's control system, which the company declines on the ground that the system is sensitive, and records that she could not visualise the shop-floor culture or the supervisors' body language.
Which combination of source-listed remote audit disadvantages is actually illustrated by these facts?
I. Time zone issues could affect efficiency
II. Remote access to sensitive IT systems may not be allowed
III. No ability to visualise facility culture and auditee body language
IV. Interviews and meetings interrupted by network issues
options: I, II and III only
I and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Fact (3) illustrates time zone issues affecting efficiency, since the overseas expert joins very late at night and discussions stretch. Fact (5) illustrates both that remote access to a designated-sensitive IT system was declined and that facility culture and body language could not be visualised, so II and III are present on the same facts. IV is not illustrated: the case never mentions network interruption of interviews or meetings, and option 4 wins by treating an unillustrated but genuine list item as present. The decisive reading is that each listed disadvantage must be tied to a specific fact, and only I, II and III are so tied here.

questions.question:
CASE: For the financial year 2025-26, CA Divya accepts the remote audit of a manufacturer based at Chandigarh, with a plant at Uttarakhand and an export warehouse at Gujarat. She: (1) agrees the audit timelines with the company and fixes Google Meet as the meeting platform, with a document sharing platform also identified; (2) ensures that access to that platform is restricted and the data encrypted, and that the information she reviews and documents is removed from the platform; (3) schedules sessions at hours convenient to India, which requires an expert seconded from the firm's overseas member network to join very late at night, with discussions stretching and efficiency affected; (4) reuses for this engagement the risk assessment she had performed and documented for last year's remote audit of a different company with similar processes; (5) seeks VPN-based remote access to the plant's control system, which the company declines on the ground that the system is sensitive, and records that she could not visualise the shop-floor culture or the supervisors' body language.
Identify the feature of Divya's approach is most clearly contrary to the source?
options: Nothing is contrary, because the risk assessment reused in (4) was performed and documented and the companies' processes were similar
The reuse in (4), since assessment should be done and documented for each audit, and an assessment from a different audit cannot be carried forward
The arrangement in (2), because removal of reviewed information from the sharing platform conflicts with the auditor's documentation duty
The use of VPN in (5), because the source requires VPN only for the document sharing platform
questions.explanation: The source's risk assessment row requires assessment to be done and documented for each audit, so the unit of compliance is each engagement and process similarity with another company does not permit carry-forward, which makes fact (4) the clear breach. Option 1 focuses on the wrong condition by treating similarity as sufficient; documentation of a prior engagement's assessment is not documentation of this one's. Option 2 is wrong because removal of information reviewed and documented by the auditor and documentation of procedures are distinct obligations that operate together, and option 3 is wrong because VPN is directed at access to the auditee's IT system rather than the sharing platform.

questions.question: CASE: An Indian audit firm accepts the remote audit of a supplier whose units are located abroad. In designing the arrangements, the company secretary proposes: (a) taking screenshots of video calls showing the auditee's personnel to prove their participation; (b) retaining on the sharing platform, permanently, all files reviewed and documented by the auditor; (c) accessing the unit's ERP over the open internet because VPN licences are unavailable; and (d) leaving platform access unrestricted since the data are encrypted. The partner also asks whether the cross-border character of the engagement matters. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate overall response?
options: Only (d) is objectionable, because a screenshot proving the personnel's participation rather than financial data falls outside the prohibition
(a), (b), (c) and (d) are each contrary to the source guidance, and the auditor should additionally take the applicable legislation and regulations into consideration
Only (c) is objectionable, because the VPN direction is unqualified and the unavailability of licences is beside the point
(b) and (d) alone are objectionable, since the sharing-platform rules do not reach the auditor's evidence-taking or the route used to access the ERP
questions.explanation: Each proposal breaches a separate limb of the confidentiality, security and data protection consideration: screenshots of auditees should not be taken as audit evidence whatever they purport to prove; information reviewed and documented by the auditor is to be removed from the platform; the auditor accessing the auditee's IT system should use VPN; and access should be restricted as well as encrypted, so encryption does not justify an unrestricted platform. The cross-border dimension is addressed by the further direction that legislation and regulations be taken into consideration, which the correct option captures and the others omit. The three rejected options are each partially correct reasoning - they identify one or two genuine breaches but treat the remaining proposals as acceptable, applying the rules too narrowly.

questions.question:
Statement 1: The comfort and flexibility available to the audit team working from a home environment and the widening of selection of auditors from a global network of experts are both placed in the source's advantages column.
Statement 2: The absence of travel time and travel costs is the stated basis for treating a remote audit as cost and time effective.
Statement 3: The unavailability of remote access to a designated-sensitive server is an advantage, since it removes the temptation for auditees to present doctored documents.
Statement 4: The interruption of interviews and meetings due to network issues and the inability to perform audit procedures like physical verification of assets and stock taking are both listed disadvantages.
options: 1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
All of the above
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 correctly allocate the listed effects: comfort and flexibility of the home environment and access to a global network of experts are advantages; cost and time effectiveness is expressly tied to no travel time and travel costs; and network interruptions and the impossibility of performing physical verification of assets and stock taking are disadvantages. Statement 3 is the trap that mixes two rows: non-permission of remote access to sensitive IT systems is a listed disadvantage, not an advantage, and the source links the doctored-document risk to a different disadvantage rather than to restricted access. The decisive test is the column in which the source itself records each effect, which rules out statement 3.

questions.question:
CASE: Sage & Co., chartered accountants, are conducting remote audits for two clients - a tea processing company at Guwahati and an ocean-freight logistics company at Kochi whose vessels are currently at sea. The following facts emerge during the engagements: (P) the audit team works from a home environment and saves travel time and travel costs; (Q) evidence gathering for the tea company is spread over three weeks instead of a compressed ten-day field visit; (R) a network outage interrupts the video exit meeting with the Kochi team; (S) the Guwahati store-keeper emails scanned invoices whose printed dates do not agree with the entries discussed, and the team cannot rule out that documents were altered while relevant papers were withheld; (T) the team is unable to visualise the facility culture of the plant or the body language of supervisors during video interviews; (U) the Kochi company's IT head declines to permit remote access to the payroll and inventory servers, which are designated as sensitive; (V) the firm inducts a port-logistics specialist from its overseas member firm into the Kochi team; (W) physical verification of the fuel on the vessels and attendance at stock taking at the Guwahati warehouse cannot be carried out.
Which of the above statements are correct?
Statement 1: (V) corresponds to the listed advantage of widening the selection of auditors from a global network of experts.
Statement 2: (S) corresponds to the listed disadvantage of increased opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information.
Statement 3: The three-week spread in (Q) resolves (W), because a longer evidence-gathering window enables the stock taking to be attended remotely.
Statement 4: (P) reflects the listed advantage that a remote audit is cost and time effective, since no travel time and travel costs are involved.
options: 1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
All of the above
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 map the facts onto the correct rows of the source table: the overseas specialist is the global network advantage, the suspect scanned invoices are the doctored documents and omission disadvantage, and the absence of travel time and cost is the cost and time effectiveness advantage. Statement 3 applies one advantage to cure a disadvantage the source treats as categorical: audit procedures like physical verification of assets and stock taking cannot be performed in a remote audit, and spreading evidence gathering over several weeks concerns document-based gathering, not enabling attendance at a count on vessels or in a warehouse. The decisive fact is that (W) is a non-performance problem, whereas (Q) is a timing benefit, so the two rows cannot be netted against each other.

questions.question:
Indira Textiles Ltd. is a power-loom weaving unit running fourteen ERP modules. During the FY 2025-26 audit, engagement partner R. Venkatesh asks his team to meet four separate needs.
Need (i): the accounts payable ledger of 6.4 lakh invoice lines must be examined for irregularities indicating fictitious vendors, and the tool selected must be one which the study material describes as a data extraction and analysis software used for fraud detection and prevention.
Need (ii): the monthly bank, inter-company and GST reconciliations, the quarterly consolidation, two system integrations and a continuous audit routine, all being set procedures performed periodically, must be carried out without repeat manual effort.
Need (iii): the audit committee, consisting mainly of non-technical independent directors, wants the findings aggregated, analysed, visualised and shared through an interactive dashboard for reporting to higher management.
Need (iv): the firm runs a standardised audit file across thirty concurrent engagements and wants to conduct these audit and assurance engagements quickly, accurately and consistently, streamlining processes and eliminating routine tasks while sharing analytical insights.
Senior associate Neha proposes Power BI for need (i) because Power BI can aggregate and analyse data, and ACL for need (iv) because ACL is the best-known audit software in the industry.
Which of the following pairing of need to tool is consistent with the descriptions given in the study material?
options: (i) CaseWare, (ii) Alteryx, (iii) Power BI, (iv) ACL
(i) ACL, (ii) Power BI, (iii) Alteryx, (iv) CaseWare
(i) ACL, (ii) Alteryx, (iii) Power BI, (iv) CaseWare
(i) Alteryx, (ii) ACL, (iii) Power BI, (iv) CaseWare
(i) ACL, (ii) Alteryx, (iii) CaseWare, (iv) Power BI
questions.explanation: The material describes ACL Analytics as a data extraction and analysis software used for fraud detection and prevention which samples large data sets to find irregularities that indicate fraud, and need (i) is stated in exactly those words. Alteryx is the tool said to consolidate financial or operational data to assess controls and to automate set procedures performed periodically such as reconciliations, consolidations, system integrations and continuous audits, which is precisely need (ii). Power BI is described as a platform for non-technical business users to aggregate, analyse, visualise and share data, with such visualisation tools used for reporting in an interactive dashboard to higher management, matching need (iii). CaseWare is described as data analysis software providing tools to conduct audit and assurance engagements quickly, accurately and consistently, sharing analytical insights and streamlining processes and eliminating routine tasks, matching need (iv). The first option misreads Neha's own proposals, which are unsupported because the material does not attach fraud detection to Power BI or the conduct of engagements to ACL.

questions.question:
